courses.title: Brake Systems: Hydraulics, Service, and ABS
courses.summary: How hydraulic brakes multiply force, how to measure and service disc brakes against OEM specifications, and how ABS/ESC and wheel speed sensors are tested. Includes brake fluid testing and scan-tool assisted bleeding.

lessons.title: Hydraulic principles and system components
lessons.body:
Every hydraulic brake system does the same job: it turns a modest push on the brake pedal into very large clamping forces at four wheels, evenly and on demand. Once you understand how that force is created and where it can be lost, most brake complaints become logical to diagnose.

## Pascal's law and force multiplication

**Pascal's law** states that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Brake fluid is treated as incompressible, so pressure created at the master cylinder appears at every caliper and wheel cylinder in that circuit.

Two relationships do the work:

- **Pressure = Force ÷ Area** — a small master cylinder piston creates high pressure from a modest force.
- **Force = Pressure × Area** — a large caliper piston converts that pressure back into a large clamping force.

**Worked example (illustrative numbers only, not specifications):**

- The driver pushes 100 lb on the pedal. A 4:1 pedal lever ratio delivers 400 lb to the pushrod (ignore the booster for now).
- The master cylinder piston area is 1 in², so line pressure is 400 ÷ 1 = **400 psi** (about 2,760 kPa or 27.6 bar).
- A caliper piston with 4 in² of area produces 400 × 4 = **1,600 lb** of clamping force.

The trade-off is **volume**. Moving a large piston a short distance requires the small master cylinder piston to travel much farther. Anything that absorbs volume — air, swelling hoses, excessive pad clearance — becomes extra pedal travel.

## System components

- **Pedal and pushrod** — the lever that provides the first stage of mechanical advantage.
- **Power booster** — multiplies driver effort. Vacuum boosters use engine vacuum or a vacuum pump; hydraulic boosters use power steering pressure; many newer vehicles use electric or integrated electro-hydraulic boosters.
- **Tandem master cylinder** — primary and secondary pistons feed two separate hydraulic circuits so a single leak does not cause total loss of braking.
- **Circuit split** — either front/rear or **diagonal** (one front wheel paired with the opposite rear wheel).
- **Lines and hoses** — rigid steel lines along the body and flexible hoses to the moving suspension.
- **Valving** — older systems use proportioning and metering valves; most modern systems perform **electronic brake-force distribution (EBD)** inside the ABS hydraulic unit.
- **Wheel brakes** — calipers on disc brakes and wheel cylinders on drum brakes.

## Reading the pedal: symptom to system

- **Spongy or soft** — air in the system, soft or swelling hoses, caliper or pad problems.
- **Low but firm** — excess clearance, rear drum adjustment, low fluid level.
- **Slowly sinks under steady pressure** — external leak, internal master cylinder bypass, ABS unit leakage.
- **Hard, high effort** — booster or booster supply fault, restricted hydraulics.

Use the pedal complaint to pick your **first test**, not your first part.

## Two quick tests before replacing anything

**Booster function check (general procedure):**

1. Engine off, pump the pedal several times to deplete the booster reserve.
2. Hold moderate, steady pressure on the pedal and start the engine.
3. The pedal should move down slightly as boost assist arrives. No movement suggests a booster or booster-supply problem; verify vacuum or pump supply against the OEM specification before condemning the booster.

**Sinking pedal check:**

1. Engine running, apply steady moderate pressure and hold for about 15–30 seconds (general guideline — verify against OEM procedure).
2. A pedal that slowly sinks with no external leak points toward internal leakage. Inspect every wheel, line, and the rear of the master cylinder for wetness first — an external leak is the most common cause.
3. Isolating the master cylinder from the ABS unit requires the OEM-approved method; do not clamp brake hoses with tools that can damage the inner lining.

## Safety

- Brake work directly affects the vehicle's ability to stop. Confirm a firm, high pedal before moving the vehicle, and road test at low speed first.
- Brake fluid irritates skin and eyes and damages paint. Wear eye protection and gloves; rinse spills with water immediately.
- Do not blow brake dust with compressed air. Use wet cleaning methods or an approved brake washer.
- Keep brake fluid free of petroleum products and dirt; contamination can swell rubber seals throughout the system.

## Key takeaways

- **Pressure = Force ÷ Area** creates high line pressure; **Force = Pressure × Area** turns it into clamping force.
- Anything that absorbs fluid volume shows up as extra pedal travel.
- Dual circuits (front/rear or diagonal) keep partial braking if one circuit fails.
- Let the pedal symptom guide the first test; verify boost and leaks before replacing the booster or master cylinder.

lessons.title: Disc brake service: thickness and runout
lessons.body:
A professional brake job is more than new pads. Most comebacks — pulsation, noise, uneven wear — come from skipped measurements and hardware shortcuts.

## Disc brake anatomy

- **Rotor** — solid or vented. The **minimum (discard) thickness** is usually cast or stamped on the rotor; the OEM may also list a separate **machine-to (refinish) thickness**.
- **Caliper** — a **floating (sliding)** caliper has piston(s) on one side and slides on pins; a **fixed** caliper has opposed pistons and does not move.
- **Pads, shims, and abutment clips** — hardware controls pad movement and noise.
- **Piston seal** — a square-cut seal that deforms during apply and pulls the piston back slightly on release (**rollback**), creating running clearance.
- **Rear parking brake** — a drum-in-hat, a mechanical caliper mechanism, or an **electronic parking brake (EPB)** caliper motor.

## Inspect before you disassemble

1. Confirm the complaint on a road test: pulsation, noise, pull, or wear warning.
2. Measure pad lining thickness at both ends of each pad and compare to the OEM minimum.
3. Read the wear pattern — it tells you *why* the pads wore:
   - **Inner pad much thinner than outer** — sticking slide pins or a piston that is not retracting.
   - **Tapered pad** — worn abutments, bracket issues, or seized hardware.
   - **One side of the axle worn more** — a caliper, hose, or hardware problem on that side.
4. Check the hoses for cracks, bulges, and twisting.

## Measuring rotor thickness and thickness variation

Use an **outside micrometer**, not a caliper-style gauge.

- Measure at several evenly spaced points (eight is a common practice) around the rotor, roughly 10 mm (3/8 in) in from the outer edge (general guideline — verify against OEM procedure).
- The **lowest** reading must meet the OEM minimum thickness. If machining would take the rotor below the refinish thickness, replace it.
- The difference between the highest and lowest readings is **thickness variation (parallelism)**. OEM limits are very tight, and thickness variation is the most common cause of pedal pulsation.

## Measuring lateral runout

Lateral runout is side-to-side wobble of the friction surface as it turns.

1. Clean the hub and rotor mounting faces — rust scale between them is a leading cause of runout.
2. Secure the rotor with lug nuts (use conical washers or adapters with the wheel off) tightened to the OEM specification with a torque wrench.
3. Mount a **dial indicator** to a rigid, non-rotating part such as the knuckle. Position the stylus perpendicular to the friction surface, about 12 mm (1/2 in) in from the outer edge (general guideline).
4. Zero the indicator at the lowest point, rotate one full turn, and record the **total indicated runout (TIR)**. Compare to the OEM specification.

If runout is excessive, remove the rotor and measure the **hub flange** alone. A hub out of specification points to the hub or bearing; a good hub points to the rotor, mounting-surface contamination, or indexing.

**Worked example (illustrative readings only):** Rotor TIR reads 0.10 mm. The bare hub reads 0.02 mm. After cleaning both faces and rotating the rotor two lug positions, TIR drops to 0.03 mm, which is now within the OEM limit for this vehicle. No parts were needed — only correct preparation.

**Why it matters:** a rotor with runout brushes the pads once per revolution even with the brakes released. Over thousands of miles this creates thickness variation — and a pulsation comeback. Measuring runout at installation prevents it.

## Caliper and hardware service

- Clean abutments to bare metal and install new clips and shims when supplied.
- Clean and lubricate slide pins with a high-temperature brake lubricant compatible with the boot rubber. Pins must slide freely by hand.
- When retracting a piston, many technicians open the bleeder and capture the displaced fluid so old fluid is not pushed back toward the ABS unit (general practice — follow OEM guidance).
- **EPB calipers:** use the scan tool service or maintenance mode to retract the parking brake before service. Never force the piston.
- Never let a caliper hang by its hose.

## Finishing the job

- Tighten caliper bolts and lug nuts to OEM specification with a torque wrench in a star pattern. Impact-only installation distorts rotors.
- Pump the pedal until it is firm **before** moving the vehicle, and check the fluid level.
- Bed in the pads using the friction manufacturer's procedure, then road test.

## Safety

- Lift and support the vehicle only at the manufacturer's lift points and use rated jack stands.
- Control brake dust with wet cleaning; never blow it off with compressed air.

## Key takeaways

- Measure rotor thickness with a micrometer at multiple points and compare to the OEM minimum and refinish specifications.
- Measure lateral runout with a dial indicator after torquing the rotor to the hub; check the hub separately when readings are high.
- Pad wear patterns reveal caliper and hardware faults that new pads alone will not fix.
- Torque lug nuts properly, restore a firm pedal, bed the pads, and road test before release.

lessons.title: ABS, ESC, and wheel speed sensor testing
lessons.body:
Anti-lock brakes (ABS) keep the wheels rotating during hard braking so the driver can still steer. Electronic stability control (ESC) builds on the same hardware to keep the vehicle pointed where the driver is steering. Both depend on accurate **wheel speed** information, so wheel speed sensor diagnosis is a core skill.

## How ABS works

The ABS module compares each wheel's speed with an estimated vehicle speed. When one wheel slows much faster than the vehicle — the beginning of lockup — the module modulates pressure to that wheel.

The **hydraulic control unit (HCU)** contains, for each channel:

- An **inlet (isolation) valve**, normally open, that can block further pressure from the master cylinder.
- An **outlet (dump) valve**, normally closed, that can release pressure to a low-pressure accumulator.
- A shared **pump motor** that returns released fluid toward the master cylinder side.

ABS cycles through three phases many times per second:

1. **Hold** — the inlet valve closes; wheel pressure stays constant.
2. **Release** — the outlet valve opens; wheel pressure drops and the wheel speeds back up.
3. **Build** — the outlet closes and the inlet reopens; pressure rises again.

Pedal pulsation and pump noise during an ABS stop are **normal**. The same hardware provides **electronic brake-force distribution (EBD)** and **traction control**, which brakes a spinning wheel and requests an engine torque reduction.

## What ESC adds

ESC compares the driver's intended path with the vehicle's actual motion using:

- A **steering angle sensor** — driver intent.
- A **yaw rate sensor** and **lateral accelerometer**, often combined in one inertial sensor.
- A **brake pressure sensor** — driver braking demand.

When the vehicle understeers or oversteers, ESC brakes individual wheels and requests torque reduction over the network. Because ESC relies on other modules, an uncalibrated steering angle sensor, a network fault, or an engine fault can disable it.

## Wheel speed sensor types

**Passive (variable reluctance) sensors**

- A coil and magnet generate an **AC voltage** as tone ring teeth pass the tip.
- Output amplitude and frequency both rise with speed; air gap matters.
- Usually two wires; the coil can be resistance-tested against the OEM specification.

**Active (Hall-effect or magnetoresistive) sensors**

- Powered by the ABS module; they output a **digital square-wave signal**, commonly as two alternating current levels.
- They read accurately down to nearly zero speed, and some report direction.
- Many read a **magnetic encoder ring** built into the wheel bearing seal.
- An ohmmeter reading is **not** a meaningful test for an active sensor.

## Diagnostic strategy

1. **Scan and document.** Record DTCs and freeze frame data. Note the vehicle speed when the code set.
2. **Check tires first.** Mismatched tire sizes, a compact spare, or very different tread depths can set wheel speed plausibility codes on a healthy system.
3. **Compare live data.** Drive straight at a steady speed and compare all four wheel speeds. A faulty channel usually drops out, reads erratically, or disagrees with the other three.
4. **Inspect.** Look at harness flex points, connector corrosion, metal debris on the sensor tip, cracked or rusted tone rings, and wheel bearing play (excess play changes the air gap).
5. **Test electrically.**
   - **Passive:** measure coil resistance and check for shorts to ground per OEM specification. With the wheel off the ground, spin it by hand and compare AC output side to side, or view the sine wave on an oscilloscope.
   - **Active:** with the ignition on, verify supply voltage at the sensor connector against OEM specification, then scope the signal (or use a low-amp current probe) while turning the wheel. Look for a clean, consistent square wave.

**Worked example:** An active sensor channel drops to zero intermittently at about 35 mph while the other three wheels agree. The scope shows a good square wave with a group of missing pulses once per wheel revolution. The sensor is producing a signal correctly — the **encoder** is damaged. Inspection finds a torn magnetic encoder seal on the bearing. The repair is a hub bearing, not a sensor. Testing prevented an unnecessary part.

## Safety

- Support the vehicle on a lift or jack stands before spinning wheels by hand.
- Avoid running driven wheels in gear on a lift unless the OEM procedure calls for it; traction control can apply the brakes unexpectedly and set codes.
- After any ABS or ESC repair, clear codes, confirm the warning lamps go out, and road test to verify.

## Key takeaways

- ABS controls wheel slip with inlet valves, outlet valves, and a pump through hold, release, and build phases.
- ESC adds steering angle, yaw rate, and lateral acceleration inputs and depends on other modules.
- Passive sensors produce AC voltage; active sensors produce a powered digital signal and cannot be judged with an ohmmeter.
- Check tires and compare all four wheel speeds before condemning any sensor; a damaged tone ring or encoder is a common root cause.

lessons.title: Brake fluid and bleeding procedures
lessons.body:
Brake fluid is a working component, not just a filler. It transmits pressure, protects internal parts from corrosion, and must resist boiling under heavy braking. This lesson covers how to evaluate fluid, choose a bleeding method, and use the scan tool when the ABS unit must be purged.

## Brake fluid types

- **DOT 3, DOT 4, and DOT 5.1** are glycol-ether based. They are **hygroscopic** — they absorb moisture from the air through hoses, seals, and the reservoir vent.
- **DOT 5** is silicone based, is rarely specified for modern vehicles, and must never be mixed with glycol fluids.
- Always use the grade specified on the reservoir cap or in the OEM service information.

The federal standard (FMVSS 116) sets minimum boiling points for each grade. These are fluid-grade minimums, not vehicle specifications:

- **DOT 3:** 205 °C (401 °F) dry, 140 °C (284 °F) wet.
- **DOT 4:** 230 °C (446 °F) dry, 155 °C (311 °F) wet.
- **DOT 5.1:** 260 °C (500 °F) dry, 180 °C (356 °F) wet.

As moisture content rises, the boiling point falls toward the wet value. Under repeated hard stops the fluid in the caliper can boil, creating vapor — the pedal suddenly goes soft. Moisture also corrodes ABS valves and caliper bores.

## Test the fluid — don't judge by color

Color alone is not a reliable test. Use a measurement:

- **Copper test strips** detect dissolved copper, a sign the corrosion inhibitors are depleted. A common industry guideline flags fluid at or above about 200 ppm copper for replacement (general guideline — verify against OEM specification).
- **Boiling point testers** heat a sample and report its actual boiling point.
- **Pen-style moisture testers** estimate water content by conductivity; they are useful for screening but less precise.

Follow the OEM service interval even when test results look acceptable.

## Bleeding methods

- **Manual (two-person):** apply the pedal, open the bleeder, close it before the pedal is released. On a master cylinder that has been in service for years, avoid pushing the pedal past its normal travel — deposits in the unused part of the bore can damage the seals (general guideline). A block under the pedal limits travel.
- **Pressure bleeding:** a pressurized adapter on the reservoir pushes fluid through the system. Use the pressure recommended by the equipment maker and the OEM.
- **Vacuum bleeding:** draws fluid out at the bleeder. Bubbles can be pulled past the bleeder threads, so do not mistake them for air in the system.
- **Gravity bleeding:** slow but gentle; useful for some component replacements.
- **Bench bleeding:** always bleed a new master cylinder before installation.

Follow the OEM **bleed sequence**. Many systems start at the wheel farthest from the master cylinder, but diagonal-split and ABS-equipped systems may differ. Never let the reservoir run low while bleeding — that is how air reaches the ABS unit.

## Scan-tool assisted (automated) bleeding

The ABS hydraulic unit contains passages, valves, and accumulators that stay closed during a normal bleed. Air trapped there can move into the brake lines during the next ABS stop, and the pedal suddenly turns spongy.

An **automated bleed** routine uses the scan tool to cycle the ABS pump and valves so trapped air is flushed toward the wheel bleeders. It is commonly required when:

- The hydraulic unit or master cylinder was replaced (unless the OEM specifies a pre-filled unit procedure).
- The reservoir ran dry or air otherwise entered the hydraulic unit.
- The OEM procedure calls for it after specific repairs.

**Typical sequence (overview — follow the OEM procedure exactly):**

1. Perform a conventional base bleed.
2. Connect a battery maintainer; low voltage can abort the routine.
3. Run the automated bleed function, applying the pedal and opening bleeders only when prompted.
4. Allow the pump motor to cool between cycles as instructed.
5. Repeat the base bleed and verify the pedal.

**Integrated and brake-by-wire systems** can build high pressure on their own when a door opens or the pedal is touched. Many require a scan tool service mode or another OEM-specified disabling step before any hydraulic connection is opened.

## Verification

- Pedal is firm and high with the engine off and running, and it does not sink.
- Bleeders are tight and dry, and the fluid is at the correct level.
- Road test, including a controlled ABS stop in a safe location if shop policy allows.

## Safety

- Brake fluid irritates skin and eyes and removes paint. Wear eye protection and gloves; dispose of used fluid as hazardous waste.
- Never move the vehicle until a firm pedal is confirmed.
- Treat self-pressurizing brake systems as stored-energy hazards until the OEM disabling procedure is complete.

## Key takeaways

- Glycol brake fluids absorb moisture, lowering the boiling point and causing corrosion.
- Test fluid with copper strips or a boiling point tester instead of judging color.
- Choose a bleeding method that suits the job, follow the OEM sequence, and never let the reservoir run dry.
- Use scan-tool automated bleeding when air may be trapped in the ABS hydraulic unit.

questions.q: A pushrod applies 600 lb to a master cylinder piston with an area of 0.75 in². What line pressure is produced (illustrative numbers)?
choices: 450 psi
800 psi
600 psi
questions.explanation: Pressure = Force ÷ Area = 600 lb ÷ 0.75 in² = 800 psi. A smaller piston area produces higher pressure from the same force.

questions.q: Engine off, the pedal is pumped to deplete the booster reserve, then held with steady pressure while the engine is started. The pedal does not move at all. What is the most logical next step?
choices: Replace the master cylinder
Bleed the brakes to remove air
Verify the booster's vacuum or pump supply against OEM specification before condemning the booster
Replace the brake light switch
questions.explanation: No pedal drop means no boost assist arrived. The booster could be faulty, but a collapsed hose, bad check valve, or weak vacuum pump produces the same result, so verify the supply first.

questions.q: On a floating caliper, the inner pad is worn much thinner than the outer pad. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Excessive rotor thickness variation
The wrong brake fluid grade
A worn wheel bearing
Sticking slide pins or a piston that is not retracting
questions.explanation: The piston pushes the inner pad directly. If the caliper cannot slide freely or the piston does not retract, the inner pad stays in contact and wears faster. New pads alone will not fix it.

questions.q: Lateral runout is high with the rotor installed, but the bare hub flange measures within specification. What should you do next?
choices: Clean both mounting faces, re-index the rotor on the hub, and re-measure
Replace the hub bearing assembly
Replace the caliper to reduce drag
Tighten the lug nuts beyond specification to pull the rotor flat
questions.explanation: A good hub points to the rotor or its mounting. Rust or debris between the faces and rotor indexing are common causes; correct them and measure again before machining or replacing the rotor.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of brake pedal pulsation during normal stops?
choices: Air trapped in the ABS unit
A weak vacuum booster
Rotor thickness variation, often developing from lateral runout
Moisture-contaminated brake fluid
questions.explanation: As a rotor with thickness variation turns, the pads are pushed in and out, which the driver feels at the pedal. Runout causes uneven pad contact that creates thickness variation over time.

questions.q: Which test is NOT a meaningful way to judge an active (Hall-effect or magnetoresistive) wheel speed sensor?
choices: Checking supply voltage at the connector with the ignition on
Measuring its resistance with an ohmmeter and calling it good or bad
Scoping the signal while turning the wheel
Comparing its live data with the other three wheels
questions.explanation: Active sensors contain electronics and are powered by the ABS module. A resistance reading does not show whether they produce a correct signal; supply voltage and signal checks do.

questions.q: A vehicle sets a wheel speed plausibility code after the customer replaced one tire and is also running a compact spare. What should be checked first?
choices: Whether tire sizes and tread depths match
The wheel speed sensor at the corner that set the code
The ABS module software level
Whether an automated bleed is needed
questions.explanation: Different rolling diameters make one wheel appear to turn faster or slower than the others. Correct the tire mismatch and recheck before testing or replacing sensors.

questions.q: During the pressure release phase of an ABS stop, what happens in the hydraulic control unit?
choices: The inlet valve opens to raise wheel pressure
Both valves close to hold wheel pressure
The master cylinder returns fluid directly to the reservoir
The outlet (dump) valve opens to lower wheel pressure
questions.explanation: In release, the normally closed outlet valve opens so fluid leaves the wheel circuit, letting the wheel speed back up. The pump then returns that fluid toward the master cylinder side.

questions.q: Why is a scan-tool automated bleed commonly required after the ABS hydraulic unit is replaced?
choices: It resets the brake pad wear indicator
It cycles the ABS pump and valves to purge air from passages a normal bleed cannot reach
It calibrates the wheel speed sensors
It measures the brake fluid boiling point
questions.explanation: Some internal passages and accumulators stay closed during a conventional bleed. Air trapped there can enter the lines during the next ABS event and cause a sudden spongy pedal.

questions.q: Which method best indicates that brake fluid's corrosion inhibitors are depleted?
choices: Comparing its color with new fluid
Checking the level against the MAX mark
Using a copper test strip
Feeling its viscosity between your fingers
questions.explanation: Dissolved copper rises as inhibitors are used up. Color changes with age and additives and is not a reliable test; level indicates wear or leaks, not fluid condition.

courses.title: Suspension Systems and Alignment
courses.summary: Identify suspension designs and components, locate noises and play with proven inspection techniques, and understand camber, caster, toe, and thrust angle for accurate alignment diagnosis.

lessons.title: Suspension designs and components
lessons.body:
The suspension supports the vehicle's weight, keeps the tires in contact with the road, controls body motion, and holds the wheels at the correct alignment angles. Before you can diagnose a noise or a wear pattern, you need to recognize the design in front of you and know what each part does.

## Sprung and unsprung weight

- **Sprung weight** is everything supported by the springs: body, frame, engine, passengers.
- **Unsprung weight** is everything not supported by the springs: wheels, tires, brakes, knuckles, and part of the arms and axles.

Lower unsprung weight lets the wheel follow the road surface more easily, which improves grip and ride.

## Common suspension designs

- **Solid (beam) axle** — both wheels are connected by one axle. It is durable and common on trucks, using leaf springs or coil springs located by links such as trailing arms and a track (Panhard) bar. A bump at one wheel affects the other.
- **Twist beam (torsion beam)** — a semi-independent rear design common on front-wheel-drive cars. Two trailing arms are joined by a beam that twists as the wheels move differently.
- **MacPherson strut** — the strut is a **structural** part that combines the damper, spring seat, and upper steering pivot. A lower control arm and ball joint locate the bottom of the knuckle. It is compact and widely used at the front.
- **Short-long arm (SLA) or double wishbone** — upper and lower control arms, with the upper arm shorter. This geometry controls camber as the suspension compresses.
- **Multilink** — several individual links locate each wheel. It allows precise tuning but has many bushings to inspect.

## Springs

- **Coil springs** — the most common type on passenger vehicles.
- **Leaf springs** — stacked steel (or composite) leaves that both support weight and locate the axle.
- **Torsion bars** — a bar that twists to act as a spring; some designs allow ride height adjustment.
- **Air springs** — rubber bladders supplied by a compressor and controlled by height sensors and a valve block. Many systems level the vehicle automatically.

## Dampers: shocks and struts

Springs store energy; **dampers** turn motion into heat so the body does not keep bouncing.

- **Twin-tube** and **monotube** designs are the most common. Monotube units usually carry a high gas charge.
- A **shock absorber** only damps motion. A **strut** also carries side loads and locates the wheel, so strut replacement usually affects alignment.
- **Adaptive dampers** change firmness electronically; some use magnetorheological fluid.

## Other key components

- **Control arms and bushings** — locate the wheel while rubber or fluid-filled bushings isolate noise and vibration.
- **Ball joints** — pivot points between arms and knuckles. A **load-carrying** joint supports vehicle weight through the spring; a **follower** joint only locates the knuckle. Some joints have a **wear indicator** checked with the weight on the wheels.
- **Stabilizer (sway) bar and links** — tie the left and right sides together to reduce body roll.
- **Strut mounts and bearings** — isolate the strut from the body and, on steering axles, let the strut rotate.
- **Jounce bumpers and dust boots** — limit travel and protect the damper rod.

**Ride height matters.** Sagging springs or incorrect air suspension height change alignment angles and can alter ADAS sensor aim. Measure ride height at the points and conditions listed in the OEM service information.

## Worked example: identify the design

A compact front-wheel-drive sedan is on the lift. At the front, a strut bolts to the strut tower at the top and clamps to the knuckle at the bottom, with one lower control arm — a **MacPherson strut** front. At the rear, a single U-shaped beam joins two trailing arms, with coil springs and separate shocks — a **twist-beam** rear. Knowing this tells you which parts can wear, which alignment angles are adjustable, and which OEM procedures apply.

## Safety

- Coil springs store a large amount of energy. Use a strut spring compressor designed for the job and **never** loosen the strut rod nut until the spring is fully compressed and captive.
- On some designs the spring pushes against the control arm. Support the arm before removing a shock, link, or ball joint.
- Air suspension can raise or lower the vehicle on its own. Disable it using the OEM procedure before lifting or servicing.
- Lift only at the manufacturer's lift points and use rated jack stands.

## Key takeaways

- Identify the suspension design first; it defines which parts can wear and which angles can be adjusted.
- Springs support weight; dampers control motion. A strut is also a structural locating component.
- Know which ball joint is load-carrying before you inspect it.
- Compressed springs and self-leveling air suspension are serious stored-energy hazards.

lessons.title: Diagnosing suspension noises and play
lessons.body:
Suspension noises are easy to hear and hard to locate. Sound travels through the body structure, so a clunk that seems to come from one place often starts somewhere else. The goal is to **find the part that is actually moving**, prove it, and replace only that part.

## Start with the complaint

Ask questions that narrow the conditions:

- **When** — over bumps, while turning, braking, accelerating, at a certain speed, only when cold?
- **What it sounds like** — clunk, knock, creak, groan, squeak, rattle, pop, or hum?
- **Where** — front or rear, left or right, felt in the floor, seat, or steering wheel?

Then road test the vehicle with the customer if possible. Use a consistent route with speed bumps, driveway angles, a rough section, and slow tight turns.

## Noise patterns (possibilities to test, not conclusions)

- **Clunk over small bumps** — stabilizer bar links or bushings, strut mounts, loose fasteners, worn control arm bushings or ball joints.
- **Creak or groan over speed bumps or when turning** — dry ball joints, stabilizer bar bushings, control arm bushings, strut bearings.
- **Pop or bind when turning at low speed** — strut mount bearing on a steering axle; may also cause the steering to not return to center.
- **Rattle on rough roads** — loose heat shields and exhaust hangers are frequent non-suspension causes.
- **Hum or growl that changes with vehicle speed** — usually a wheel bearing or tires. Suspension movement does not cause speed-related hum.

## Inspection tools and techniques

**Visual inspection**

- Torn boots, cracked or displaced bushings, broken springs, bent arms, and missing fasteners.
- **Shiny rub marks** where metal has been contacting metal.
- Dampers: a light film may be normal on some designs, but active fluid dripping or a wet, dirt-caked body indicates failure.

**Listening tools**

- **Electronic listening devices (chassis ears)** clip to suspect components during a road test so you can compare channels.
- A mechanic's **stethoscope** while an assistant bounces the vehicle.

**Play checks**

- **Dry-park check:** with the vehicle's weight on the tires, have an assistant rock the steering wheel back and forth while you watch and feel each steering joint for lost motion.
- **Wheel shake check (wheel off the ground):** grip the tire at 12 and 6 o'clock and rock it. Play here suggests a ball joint or wheel bearing. Have an assistant apply the brakes — if the play disappears, suspect the wheel bearing; if it remains, suspect the ball joint or bushings.
- Grip at 3 and 9 o'clock to check tie rod ends and steering linkage.
- **Pry bar checks:** apply controlled leverage to bushings and joints and watch for movement.
- **Ball joints:** unload the joint as the OEM procedure describes, then measure play with a dial indicator and compare to the OEM specification. Wear-indicator joints are checked with the vehicle on the ground.

## Tire wear tells a story

- **Cupping or scalloping** — worn dampers, imbalance, or looseness.
- **Feathered tread** — incorrect toe.
- **One shoulder worn** — camber or toe problem; look for bent or worn parts before aligning.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** clunk from the front over small bumps at low speed.

1. The road test confirms the noise, loudest on the left front.
2. The visual inspection finds nothing obvious.
3. Chassis ears go on the left stabilizer link, the strut mount, and the lower ball joint. On the next road test, the stabilizer link channel is clearly loudest.
4. On the lift, a pry bar check shows free play at the link's ball stud.
5. The link is replaced and tightened at the OEM-specified suspension position, and a final road test confirms the noise is gone.

The strut the customer suspected was never replaced — the test identified the real cause.

**Tip:** many rubber bushings must be tightened with the suspension at normal ride height. Tightening them with the suspension hanging preloads the rubber and shortens its life.

## Safety

- Support the vehicle properly on a lift or rated jack stands before any play check.
- Be aware of stored spring energy when disconnecting links, arms, or dampers; support the arm first.
- Keep hands clear of pinch points while an assistant rocks the steering wheel or bounces the vehicle.

## Key takeaways

- Define when, what, and where before touching a tool, then reproduce the noise on a road test.
- Use chassis ears, a stethoscope, and play checks to **prove** which part is moving.
- Use brake application during the wheel shake check to separate wheel bearing play from ball joint play.
- Tire wear patterns point to underlying suspension or alignment problems that must be fixed first.

lessons.title: Alignment angles: camber, caster, and toe
lessons.body:
Wheel alignment is the set of angles that control how the tires meet the road. Correct alignment gives straight tracking, a centered steering wheel, and even tire wear. An alignment machine can measure these angles precisely, but **you** must understand what each angle does to interpret the numbers and find the real problem.

## Before you align: pre-checks

An alignment on worn or incorrect parts will not hold. Verify first:

- Tire pressures, sizes, and condition match on each axle.
- **Ride height** is within the OEM specification — sagging springs change camber and toe.
- Steering and suspension joints have no excessive play.
- Heavy cargo is removed, unless the OEM procedure specifies a load.

## Camber

**Camber** is the inward or outward tilt of the top of the tire viewed from the front.

- **Positive camber:** top of the tire tilts outward. **Negative camber:** top tilts inward.
- Excessive camber wears one shoulder of the tire.
- A side-to-side difference (**cross-camber**) can make the vehicle pull toward the side with more positive camber.
- Many MacPherson designs have little or no camber adjustment. An out-of-specification reading often points to bent or shifted parts.

## Caster

**Caster** is the forward or rearward tilt of the steering axis viewed from the side.

- **Positive caster:** the top of the steering axis tilts toward the rear of the vehicle.
- Positive caster provides straight-line stability and helps the steering wheel return to center.
- Caster by itself causes little tire wear, but a side-to-side difference (**cross-caster**) can cause a pull toward the side with **less** positive caster.
- Caster that is out of specification on a non-adjustable design usually means something is bent or a mounting point has shifted.

## Toe

**Toe** is the difference in distance between the front and rear of the tires on the same axle, viewed from above.

- **Toe-in:** the fronts of the tires are closer together. **Toe-out:** the fronts are farther apart.
- Toe is the most important **tire-wear angle**. Incorrect toe drags the tires sideways and produces a **feathered** wear pattern.
- Front toe is adjusted at the tie rods; many independent rear suspensions have adjustable rear toe.

## Thrust angle and diagnostic angles

- **Thrust angle** is the direction the rear wheels point relative to the vehicle's centerline. A thrust angle out of specification makes the vehicle track at an angle and leaves the steering wheel off center even when front toe looks correct.
- **Steering axis inclination (SAI)** is the inward tilt of the steering axis viewed from the front.
- **Included angle** is SAI plus camber. Comparing SAI, camber, and included angle side to side helps identify whether a knuckle or strut is bent or whether a control arm or mounting point has moved. Use the diagnostic chart in the OEM or alignment equipment documentation.

## Pull diagnosis

A pull is not always alignment. Check, in order:

1. **Tires** — swap the front tires side to side. If the pull changes direction, a tire (radial pull or conicity) is the cause.
2. **Brakes** — a dragging caliper can cause a pull while cruising.
3. **Cross-camber and cross-caster** from the alignment readings.
4. **Road crown** — a slight drift with the slope of the road can be normal.

## Alignment sequence

1. Set the **rear** first (camber, then toe) if adjustable, because the rear defines the thrust line.
2. Set front **caster**, then **camber**, then **toe**.
3. Center the steering wheel by adjusting the tie rods — never by moving the wheel on its splines.
4. Perform any required **steering angle sensor** or **ADAS calibration** per OEM procedure, then road test.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** steering wheel is off center when driving straight after the vehicle hit a curb. There is no pull.

- Front camber and caster are within specification. Front toe is within specification relative to the thrust line.
- The **thrust angle** is out of specification, and left rear toe is far from the right.
- Inspection finds a bent left rear toe link. After replacing it, rear toe is set, front toe is reset to the new thrust line, and the steering wheel is centered.
- The steering angle sensor is recalibrated per OEM procedure, and the road test confirms a centered wheel.

The rear readings, not the front, revealed the damaged part.

## Safety

- Chock the vehicle and lock the alignment rack at the correct height before working underneath.
- Keep turntable and slip-plate locking pins installed until the vehicle is positioned.
- Keep hands clear of steering components while an assistant turns the wheel.

## Key takeaways

- Verify tires, ride height, and worn parts before aligning.
- Camber and toe affect tire wear; caster affects stability and returnability; cross-camber and cross-caster can cause pulls.
- Toe is the primary tire-wear angle; thrust angle explains many off-center steering wheels.
- Align rear first, then caster, camber, and toe, and complete any required sensor calibrations.

questions.q: Which suspension design uses a structural strut that also serves as the upper steering pivot, with a single lower control arm?
choices: Solid axle with leaf springs
Twist beam
MacPherson strut
Multilink
questions.explanation: In a MacPherson design the strut carries side loads and locates the top of the knuckle, so replacing it usually affects alignment.

questions.q: A customer asks for new struts because the vehicle feels bouncy. Which finding best supports a worn damper?
choices: A light oil film on the strut body
Cupped tire wear and fluid actively dripping from the damper
A clunk only at full steering lock
A steering wheel that is off center
questions.explanation: Active leakage plus cupped wear is solid evidence of lost damping. A light film can be normal on some designs, and the other symptoms point to different systems.

questions.q: With the wheel off the ground, you feel play when rocking the tire at 12 and 6 o'clock. When an assistant applies the brakes, the play disappears. What is most likely worn?
choices: The lower ball joint
The outer tie rod end
The stabilizer link
The wheel bearing
questions.explanation: Applying the brakes locks the hub to the knuckle, taking bearing play out of the check. Play that disappears is in the bearing; play that remains is in the ball joint or bushings.

questions.q: A hum rises and falls with vehicle speed and does not change over bumps. Which is the most likely source?
choices: A wheel bearing or the tires
A stabilizer bar link
A strut mount
A control arm bushing
questions.explanation: Speed-related hum comes from rotating parts. Suspension joints and bushings make noise when the suspension moves, not in proportion to road speed.

questions.q: Why does the OEM often specify tightening rubber suspension bushings with the suspension at normal ride height?
choices: To set the camber angle automatically
To reduce wheel bearing endplay
To avoid preloading the rubber, which shortens bushing life
Because the threads engage fully only at ride height
questions.explanation: Rubber bushings twist rather than rotate. Clamping them with the suspension hanging leaves them twisted at ride height, causing premature failure and possibly a ride height change.

questions.q: Which alignment angle is considered the primary tire-wear angle and typically causes a feathered tread pattern?
choices: Toe
Caster
Steering axis inclination
Thrust angle
questions.explanation: Incorrect toe scrubs the tire sideways as it rolls, producing a feathered or saw-tooth pattern across the tread.

questions.q: A vehicle pulls to the right. After the front tires are swapped side to side, it pulls to the left. What is the cause?
choices: Tire conicity or radial pull
Cross-caster
A dragging right front caliper
Road crown
questions.explanation: If the pull follows the tires, a tire is responsible. Alignment, brake, and road crown causes would not change direction when the tires are swapped.

questions.q: The steering wheel is off center when driving straight, there is no pull, and front toe is within specification relative to the thrust line. Which reading most likely explains it?
choices: Front caster
Thrust angle out of specification
Steering axis inclination
Front camber
questions.explanation: When the rear wheels steer the vehicle at an angle, the driver must turn the steering wheel to go straight. Correct the rear toe or damaged rear parts first.

questions.q: With a cross-caster difference between the front wheels, the vehicle tends to pull toward which side?
choices: The side with more positive caster
Always toward the road crown
Caster differences never cause a pull
The side with less positive caster
questions.explanation: A vehicle tends to pull toward the side with less positive caster. Caster that is out of specification on a non-adjustable design usually indicates bent or shifted parts.

questions.q: What is the correct general sequence for a four-wheel alignment?
choices: Front toe, front camber, then rear toe
Rear camber and toe, then front caster, camber, and toe
Front caster, rear toe, then front camber
Toe on all four wheels first, then camber
questions.explanation: The rear sets the thrust line, so it is adjusted first. Front caster and camber affect toe, so front toe is set last and the steering wheel is centered with the tie rods.

courses.title: Steering Systems and EPS Diagnostics
courses.summary: Rack-and-pinion, hydraulic, and electric power steering operation, a structured approach to steering complaints, and steering angle sensor calibration with the SRS precautions that go with it.

lessons.title: Rack-and-pinion and electric power steering
lessons.body:
The steering system turns the driver's input into a precise change in wheel angle. Modern steering also supports driver-assistance features, so the steering gear is now both a mechanical assembly and an electronic actuator. This lesson covers how rack-and-pinion steering, hydraulic assist, and electric power steering (EPS) work.

## The steering path

Driver input travels through:

1. **Steering wheel** — with the driver airbag, clockspring, and often the steering angle sensor behind it.
2. **Steering column and intermediate shaft** — universal joints carry rotation around obstacles to the steering gear.
3. **Steering gear** — converts rotation into side-to-side motion.
4. **Tie rods** — connect the gear to the steering arms on the knuckles.

## Rack-and-pinion steering

- The **pinion** gear on the input shaft meshes with teeth on the **rack**. Turning the pinion slides the rack left or right.
- **Inner tie rods** are ball sockets threaded onto the rack ends; **outer tie rod ends** connect to the knuckles and are used to adjust toe.
- **Bellows boots** keep dirt and water out of the rack.
- A spring-loaded **rack yoke (support)** holds the rack against the pinion to control lash.
- **Rack mounting bushings** hold the gear to the subframe; worn bushings let the whole rack shift.

**Steering ratio** is how many degrees the steering wheel turns for each degree of road wheel movement. Some racks use a **variable ratio**, quicker off center.

Many trucks use a **recirculating-ball** gearbox with a pitman arm and parallelogram linkage instead of a rack.

## Hydraulic power steering

- A belt-driven **pump** supplies fluid through a flow-control and pressure-relief valve.
- A **rotary valve** with a **torsion bar** senses driver effort. As the bar twists, the valve directs pressure to one side of a piston on the rack.
- **Electro-hydraulic** systems replace the belt drive with an electric motor-driven pump.

## Electric power steering (EPS)

EPS replaces hydraulics with an electric motor. Common layouts:

- **Column assist** — motor and reduction gear on the steering column; common on smaller vehicles.
- **Pinion assist** — motor drives the pinion or a second pinion on the rack.
- **Rack assist** — motor drives the rack through a belt and ball-nut; used on larger, heavier vehicles.

Key components:

- **Torque sensor** — measures twist in a torsion bar to calculate driver effort. It usually outputs redundant signals so the module can detect faults.
- **Assist motor** — typically brushless, with its own position sensor.
- **EPS control module** — calculates assist from driver torque, **vehicle speed**, and other network inputs. Assist is higher at parking speeds and lower at highway speeds.

Because the module can apply torque on its own, EPS enables **lane keeping assist, park assist, and pull compensation**. That also means EPS depends on the network, the steering angle sensor, and correct calibrations.

## Power supply matters

An EPS motor draws high current during parking maneuvers. Low battery voltage, a weak charging system, or a high-resistance power or ground connection can cause **reduced assist** warnings and codes.

Many EPS modules also reduce assist temporarily to protect themselves from overheating after extended parking maneuvers. That can be **normal** operation, not a failure.

**Worked example:** a customer reports heavy steering in parking lots, especially on cold mornings. The EPS module stores a low-voltage code. A battery test shows a weak battery, and a voltage drop test on the EPS ground while turning the wheel at a standstill shows excessive loss at a corroded ground eyelet. Cleaning the ground and replacing the tested-bad battery restores normal assist. The steering gear was never the problem.

## Safety

- Column and steering wheel work often involves the **SRS (airbag)** system and clockspring. Follow the OEM SRS disabling procedure before disconnecting any column component.
- Support the vehicle properly on a lift or rated jack stands when inspecting the rack, boots, and tie rods.
- An EPS system can move the steering wheel on its own during tests or calibrations. Keep hands and tools clear.

## Key takeaways

- Rack-and-pinion gears convert pinion rotation into rack movement; tie rods transfer it to the knuckles.
- Hydraulic assist uses a torsion bar and rotary valve to direct pressure; EPS uses a torque sensor and an electric motor.
- EPS assist depends on vehicle speed, network data, and a healthy power supply.
- Test battery, charging, and EPS power and ground circuits before condemning an EPS gear.

lessons.title: Diagnosing steering complaints
lessons.body:
Steering complaints often overlap with suspension, tire, and alignment problems. A structured approach separates the **assist system** from the **mechanical linkage** and the **tires**, so you only replace what is proven faulty.

## Classify the complaint

- **Hard steering** — in both directions, one direction, only when cold, or intermittently.
- **Loose steering or wander** — the driver constantly corrects to stay in the lane.
- **Pull or drift** — often tires, brakes, or alignment (see the suspension alignment lesson).
- **Shimmy or vibration** — usually tires and wheels, sometimes worn linkage.
- **Noise** — whine, groan, clunk, knock, or squeal.
- **Poor return to center** — the wheel stays turned after a corner.
- **Warning lamp or reduced assist** — an EPS or network-related fault.

## First checks for every complaint

1. Tire pressures, sizes, and condition.
2. **Hydraulic systems:** fluid level, condition, and aeration (foamy fluid); drive belt condition and tension.
3. **EPS systems:** battery state of charge and charging system output.
4. Scan all modules. EPS, ABS/ESC, and steering angle sensor codes are often related.

## Hard steering: assist or mechanical?

**Isolate mechanical binding first.** With the front wheels off the ground and the vehicle safely supported, turn the steering slowly from lock to lock with the engine off. A notchy or binding feel points to a mechanical cause:

- Intermediate shaft universal joints.
- Strut mount bearings or seized ball joints.
- An internally damaged steering gear.

**Hydraulic assist testing.** Install a power steering analyzer (pressure gauge, flow meter, and shutoff valve) in the pressure line.

- Compare flow and pressure at idle and during turns to the OEM specification.
- Close the valve only briefly — a few seconds at most (general guideline — verify against OEM procedure) — to check maximum relief pressure.
- **Low pressure with the valve closed** points to the pump. **Good pump pressure but low pressure during a turn** points to internal leakage in the gear.

**EPS testing.** Use scan tool data:

- **Torque sensor** — near zero with hands off, changing smoothly and symmetrically left and right.
- **Motor current and assist status** — look for reduced assist or thermal protection flags.
- **Supply voltage** — compare battery voltage with the voltage the module reports during a stationary turn.
- Perform voltage drop tests on the EPS power and ground circuits under load.

## Loose steering and wander

- Perform a **dry-park check**: weight on the tires, an assistant rocks the steering wheel, and you watch each joint for lost motion.
- Check **inner tie rods** by squeezing the boot and feeling the inner socket while the wheel is rocked.
- Watch the **rack mounting bushings** — if the rack housing moves, the bushings are worn.
- Check outer tie rod ends, wheel bearings, and the toe setting.

## Noises

- **Whine that rises with steering effort** — low fluid, aeration, or a worn hydraulic pump.
- **Clunk when turning or over bumps felt in the wheel** — intermediate shaft, rack bushings, tie rods, or strut mounts.
- **Squeal when turning** — belt slip under hydraulic pump load.
- A light whirring from an EPS motor during parking can be normal; compare with a known-good vehicle.

## Poor return to center

Common causes include binding strut bearings or ball joints, low caster from bent parts, and EPS calibration issues such as an uncalibrated torque sensor or steering angle sensor.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** steering is heavy when turning left in parking lots but normal to the right (hydraulic system).

1. Fluid level and condition are correct with no aeration, and the belt is good.
2. With the wheels off the ground and the engine off, the steering turns smoothly lock to lock — no mechanical binding.
3. The analyzer shows pump flow and relief pressure within the OEM specification with the valve closed — **the pump is good**.
4. During a left turn, working pressure stays well below what the system reaches turning right, and effort rises. That points to internal leakage in the steering gear (valve or piston seal) for that direction.

The steering gear is replaced, bled per OEM procedure, and retested in both directions. The pump — the part many would have replaced first — was proven good and left in place.

## Safety

- Keep hands, tools, and clothing clear of belts and fans with the engine running.
- Power steering fluid and lines get hot; allow them to cool or wear protection.
- Do not hold a hydraulic system at full lock for extended periods.
- Support the vehicle correctly before any off-the-ground checks.

## Key takeaways

- Classify the complaint, then check tires, fluid or electrical supply, and codes first.
- Turn the steering with the wheels off the ground to separate mechanical binding from assist problems.
- Use pressure and flow testing for hydraulic systems and live data plus voltage drop testing for EPS.
- Prove looseness with dry-park and inner tie rod checks before replacing parts.

lessons.title: Steering angle sensor calibration
lessons.body:
The steering angle sensor (SAS) tells the vehicle where the driver is steering. Stability control, lane keeping, adaptive headlights, and park assist all depend on it. After many common repairs the sensor's **zero point** must be recalibrated, and skipping that step causes warning lamps, unwanted stability interventions, and comebacks.

## What the SAS does

- Reports steering wheel **angle** and often **rate of turn** over the network.
- **ESC** compares SAS angle (driver intent) with yaw rate and lateral acceleration (actual motion). An incorrect zero makes ESC believe the vehicle is sliding when it is not.
- **ADAS** lane keeping and lane centering use the angle to plan steering corrections.
- **EPS** uses it for return-to-center and active assist features.

The SAS may be part of the clockspring assembly, a separate sensor on the column, or built into the EPS system. Some sensors report absolute angle at all times; others must be **initialized** after a power loss, often by turning the wheel from lock to lock.

## When calibration is required

Always follow the OEM service information. Common triggers include:

- **Wheel alignment** or any toe adjustment.
- Replacing the SAS, clockspring, steering column, steering gear, or tie rods.
- Suspension repairs that change toe or thrust angle.
- Replacing or reprogramming the ABS/ESC or EPS module.
- A battery disconnect on some systems.
- A stored code indicating the SAS is not calibrated or its signal is implausible.

## Preconditions: get the vehicle right first

- Alignment must be within specification and the **steering wheel centered** while driving straight. Center the wheel with a toe adjustment — never calibrate the sensor to hide an off-center steering wheel.
- Vehicle on a level surface with the wheels pointed straight ahead.
- Battery voltage supported with a maintainer; low voltage can abort a calibration.
- Other related codes diagnosed first. A network fault or failed sensor will not be fixed by calibration.

## Calibration methods

Methods vary by manufacturer:

- **Scan tool routine** — the most common. Select the SAS zero-point or steering angle reset function, center the wheel, and follow the prompts. Some routines then ask you to turn lock to lock.
- **Self-calibration** — some systems learn center after driving straight at a steady speed for a distance.
- **Manual sequence** — a few systems use an ignition and steering sequence. Use one only when the OEM documents it for that vehicle.

## Verify the result

1. In live data, the SAS should read approximately **zero degrees** with the wheels straight, within the OEM tolerance.
2. Turn left and right slowly. The value should change smoothly in the correct direction with no jumps or dropouts.
3. Clear codes in all modules and confirm the ESC and traction lamps are off.
4. Road test with gentle turns. Compare SAS angle, yaw rate, and lateral acceleration in data if a complaint remains.

**Worked example:** after an alignment, the ESC and traction lamps are on and ESC stores a code for SAS not calibrated. Live data shows a significant angle reading with the wheels straight. The technician confirms the steering wheel is centered on a road test, runs the scan tool zero-point calibration, and verifies the reading is now near zero and changes correctly in both directions. The codes clear and stay clear. No sensor replacement was needed.

**Second example:** a vehicle's ESC applies a brake briefly on a gentle highway curve. The SAS was calibrated with the steering wheel off center before a toe correction. Recalibrating after centering the wheel corrects the unwanted intervention.

## Clockspring and SRS precautions

Many SAS units are behind the steering wheel with the driver airbag and clockspring.

- Follow the OEM **SRS disabling procedure** before removing the steering wheel or airbag: disconnect the battery as directed and wait the specified time.
- Carry a live airbag module with the trim facing away from you, and set it down trim side up.
- **Center the clockspring** as the OEM describes before installation. An off-center clockspring can break its ribbon cable when the wheel reaches full lock, causing airbag lamp, horn, or switch faults.
- Never probe SRS connectors or airbag modules with a test light or meter.

## Safety

- The EPS or ESC system may move the steering or apply brakes during calibration and road tests. Keep hands clear and choose a safe test route.
- Treat all SRS components as live until the OEM disabling procedure is complete.

## Key takeaways

- ESC, ADAS, and EPS rely on an accurate SAS zero point.
- Calibrate after alignments and steering or module repairs — but only after the alignment is correct and the steering wheel is centered.
- Verify with live data, cleared codes, and a road test.
- Respect SRS procedures and clockspring centering whenever the steering wheel is removed.

questions.q: In a rack-and-pinion steering gear, what converts steering wheel rotation into side-to-side movement?
choices: The pitman arm
The pinion gear meshing with the rack teeth
The idler arm
The torsion bar in the column
questions.explanation: The pinion on the input shaft drives the toothed rack left and right. Pitman and idler arms belong to recirculating-ball systems with parallelogram linkage.

questions.q: In an EPS system, which input most directly tells the module how much assist the driver is requesting?
choices: The steering angle sensor
The yaw rate sensor
The torque sensor measuring torsion bar twist
The wheel speed sensors
questions.explanation: Driver effort twists the torsion bar; the torque sensor measures that twist. Vehicle speed then scales the assist, and steering angle supports return-to-center and ADAS functions.

questions.q: Steering becomes heavier after several minutes of repeated parking maneuvers and returns to normal after a short drive. Power and ground voltage drop tests pass and no hard faults are stored. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Normal EPS thermal protection temporarily reducing assist
A failed torque sensor
Low power steering fluid
An incorrect toe setting
questions.explanation: EPS modules reduce assist to protect the motor and electronics from overheating during sustained high-load use. With good power supply tests and no faults, this is expected behavior to explain to the customer.

questions.q: With the front wheels off the ground and the engine off, the steering feels notchy at certain points as it is turned. Where should you look first?
choices: EPS module software
Battery state of charge
Mechanical binding such as intermediate shaft U-joints or strut bearings
Torque sensor calibration
questions.explanation: With no assist and no tire load, a notchy feel is mechanical. Binding U-joints, strut bearings, or a damaged gear cause it; electrical or calibration problems do not.

questions.q: During a hydraulic power steering test, pressure with the analyzer shutoff valve briefly closed is below the OEM relief specification. What does this indicate?
choices: Internal leakage in the steering gear
A weak pump or faulty relief valve
Worn inner tie rods
An incorrect toe setting
questions.explanation: Closing the valve isolates the gear, so the reading shows what the pump and relief valve can produce. Good relief pressure but low pressure during turns would point to the gear instead.

questions.q: Why should the steering angle sensor never be calibrated while the steering wheel is off center during straight-ahead driving?
choices: It will damage the clockspring
The ESC module will lock permanently
The sensor can only be calibrated once
It hides the alignment problem, and the zero point will be wrong once the steering wheel is centered
questions.explanation: The customer's off-center wheel remains, and when the toe is corrected later, the stored zero no longer matches straight ahead. Center the wheel with toe first, then calibrate.

questions.q: After an alignment, the ESC lamp is on and a code indicates the steering angle sensor is not calibrated. What is the best first action?
choices: Replace the steering angle sensor
Confirm the steering wheel is centered, run the OEM zero-point calibration, and verify in live data
Replace the ESC module
Disconnect the battery to reset all modules
questions.explanation: Toe changes during an alignment require a new zero point. Calibration and verification fix the fault without parts; disconnecting the battery does not calibrate the sensor.

questions.q: What can happen if a clockspring is installed without being centered?
choices: Its ribbon cable can break at full lock, causing airbag lamp, horn, or switch faults
The ESC calibrates to the wrong direction
The steering rack binds
The tie rods loosen
questions.explanation: The clockspring's ribbon has a limited number of turns in each direction. If it starts off center, turning to one lock stretches and breaks the ribbon.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a dry-park check?
choices: To test hydraulic pump pressure
To calibrate the steering angle sensor
To test the torque sensor output
To find lost motion in steering joints with the vehicle's weight on the tires
questions.explanation: With weight on the tires, rocking the steering wheel loads the linkage so worn tie rods, rack bushings, and joints show visible free play.

questions.q: A hydraulic system whines louder as steering effort increases, and the fluid in the reservoir is foamy. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Aeration from low fluid or air drawn in on the suction side
Worn inner tie rods
An uncalibrated steering angle sensor
Worn rack mounting bushings
