courses.title: ADAS Sensors and Calibration
courses.summary: How ADAS cameras, radar, lidar, and ultrasonic sensors work, when static and dynamic calibrations are required, and how to plan, sequence, verify, and document ADAS work after repairs and collisions.

lessons.title: ADAS sensors: camera, radar, lidar, and ultrasonic
lessons.body:
Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) use cameras, radar, lidar, and ultrasonic sensors to warn the driver or help control the vehicle. Most current systems are **driver support** features (SAE driving automation Levels 1 and 2): the driver remains responsible at all times. For the technician, ADAS means one thing above all — **sensors must see correctly and point exactly where the system expects**.

## Common features and the sensors behind them

- **Forward collision warning and automatic emergency braking (AEB)** — forward camera, front radar, or both.
- **Adaptive cruise control (ACC)** — front radar, often combined with the camera.
- **Lane departure warning, lane keeping, and lane centering** — forward camera, acting through the EPS system.
- **Blind spot monitoring and rear cross-traffic alert** — rear corner radars.
- **Park assist and parking sensors** — ultrasonic sensors, often with cameras.
- **Surround view** — cameras in the grille, mirrors, and tailgate.
- **Automatic high beams and adaptive headlights** — camera and steering angle inputs.

## Cameras

- The **forward-facing camera** usually sits behind the windshield near the mirror. It may be a single (mono) or stereo camera.
- It recognizes lane markings, vehicles, pedestrians, and traffic signs.
- Its view depends on the **windshield**: glass optical quality, bracket position, and a clean, undamaged area in front of the lens.
- Glare, darkness, heavy rain, and dirty glass reduce performance.

## Radar

- Radar transmits radio waves and measures the reflection to find **distance, relative speed, and angle** to objects.
- Front radars usually mount behind the grille emblem or bumper cover; corner radars mount behind the bumper corners.
- Most current automotive radars operate in the 76–81 GHz band; some older systems used 24 GHz.
- Radar works well in darkness and fog, but it is sensitive to **mounting angle**, bumper cover **paint thickness and type**, emblem design, and mud, snow, or ice on the cover.

**Worked example — why aim matters:** a radar aimed just **1°** off at an object **100 m** ahead is looking at a point about 100 × tan(1°) ≈ **1.7 m** to the side — roughly half a lane width. A bracket bent slightly in a minor collision can make the system track the wrong vehicle or miss the right one.

## Lidar

- Lidar measures distance with laser pulses and can build a detailed three-dimensional picture.
- It is less common on mainstream vehicles; some use a short-range unit near the windshield for low-speed emergency braking.
- Dirt, rain, and snow on the lens reduce performance.

## Ultrasonic sensors

- Mounted in the bumpers, they measure short distances with sound pulses at low speeds.
- Mounting angle, the correct holder, and paint thickness on the sensor face all affect accuracy.
- Ice, mud, and aftermarket accessories near the sensors cause false or missed warnings.

## Sensor fusion and supporting inputs

ADAS modules combine data from several sensors (**sensor fusion**) and rely on other systems:

- Wheel speed, yaw rate, and steering angle from the ABS/ESC system.
- Engine torque and brake control over the network.
- Ride height and alignment, which set the sensor's reference to the road.

A fault in a supporting system can disable ADAS features. For example, a stability control fault often disables adaptive cruise. **Always scan all modules**, not just the ADAS module.

## Things that commonly interfere

- Snow, mud, or bugs over sensors, which usually produces a "sensor blocked" message — often normal.
- Aftermarket license plate frames, grille guards, window tint strips, and dash cameras in the camera's view.
- Lift or lowering kits and larger tires, which change sensor aim relative to the road.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** "Adaptive cruise unavailable" and a front radar blocked message during winter driving.

1. Inspection finds slush packed over the radar area of the bumper. After cleaning, the feature works.
2. If the message had returned on a clean, dry vehicle, the next steps would be to scan for codes, inspect the radar and bracket for damage, and check whether the OEM calls for a calibration.

## Key takeaways

- Most ADAS features are driver support; the driver remains responsible.
- Cameras depend on the windshield; radar depends on mounting angle and a clear, radar-transparent cover.
- A small aim error becomes a large error at a distance.
- ADAS relies on wheel speed, yaw, steering angle, and ride height — scan every module and verify supporting systems.

lessons.title: Static and dynamic calibration
lessons.body:
An ADAS sensor must know exactly where it is pointing relative to the vehicle's direction of travel. **Calibration** teaches the sensor its actual mounting angle so the system can correct for it. Knowing **when** a calibration is required and **how** to set it up correctly is now part of everyday repair work.

## Why calibration is needed

- Every sensor, bracket, bumper, and windshield has manufacturing tolerances.
- Replacing or removing a part changes the sensor's position slightly.
- Suspension and alignment changes move the vehicle's **thrust line** — the direction the vehicle actually travels.
- As the previous lesson showed, a 1° error becomes about 1.7 m of lateral error at 100 m.

## Static calibration

Static calibration is performed in the shop with the vehicle stationary.

- **Targets or reflectors** are placed at a specified distance, height, and offset from the vehicle's centerline or thrust line.
- A frame with lasers or measuring aids positions the targets. The scan tool commands the sensor to view them and calculate its offset.
- The correct target for the specific vehicle and sensor must be used.

Static calibration demands a controlled environment:

- A **level floor** within the OEM tolerance and enough open space around the vehicle and targets.
- **Controlled lighting** for cameras — no direct sunlight, bright reflections, or patterned backgrounds in view.
- For radar, **no metal objects or reflective surfaces** in the sensor's field of view.

## Dynamic calibration

Dynamic calibration is performed by driving the vehicle.

- The scan tool starts the procedure, then the vehicle is driven at specified speeds for a specified time or distance.
- The camera needs **clear lane markings**; radar needs roadside objects and traffic to learn from.
- Weather, traffic, and road conditions affect how quickly it completes.

Some vehicles need **both** a static and a dynamic procedure. Others continuously **self-calibrate** during normal driving but still require a service procedure after certain repairs. Some radars also need **mechanical aiming** with adjusting screws before the electronic calibration.

## When calibration is required

Requirements differ by manufacturer, model, and model year, so check the OEM service information and position statements for every vehicle. Common triggers include:

- **Windshield replacement** on vehicles with a forward camera.
- Removing or replacing a camera, radar, lidar, ultrasonic sensor, or its bracket.
- Removing or replacing a bumper cover or grille that houses a sensor.
- **Wheel alignment**, or suspension work that changes ride height or thrust angle.
- Collision damage, even when the sensor area looks undamaged.
- Steering angle sensor calibration, module replacement, or software updates.
- DTCs indicating a sensor is misaligned or not calibrated.

## Pre-calibration checklist

1. **Scan all modules** and repair unrelated faults first. Calibrations often refuse to start with active codes.
2. Confirm the **correct parts** are installed — windshield type, bracket, emblem, and bumper cover.
3. Set **tire pressures** and confirm matching tire sizes.
4. Verify **ride height** and **wheel alignment**, especially thrust angle.
5. Prepare the vehicle as the procedure states: fuel level, cargo removed, doors closed, no occupants unless specified.
6. Clean the sensors and the windshield area in front of the camera.
7. Connect a **battery maintainer**; low voltage can abort the procedure.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** after a windshield replacement, lane keeping is inoperative and a camera code indicates the camera is not calibrated.

1. The new windshield is confirmed to be the correct type, and the camera bracket is secure.
2. An alignment check finds the thrust angle within specification.
3. On a level floor with controlled lighting, the target is placed at the distance and height specified for this vehicle, and the static calibration completes successfully.
4. A road test confirms the system detects lane markings and the warning lamp stays off.

## Documentation

Record everything:

- Pre-repair and post-repair scan reports.
- The calibration report or scan tool result.
- Setup measurements, floor level check, and photos of the target placement.
- The OEM procedure followed.

This documentation protects the customer and the shop and proves the vehicle left with working safety systems.

## Safety

- Dynamic calibration and verification drives take place in real traffic. Obey traffic laws, use a second person to operate the scan tool, and stay alert — an uncalibrated system may brake or steer unexpectedly.
- Never test automatic emergency braking by driving toward real obstacles. Use OEM verification procedures.
- Keep targets and stands stable and out of walkways.

## Key takeaways

- Static calibration uses precisely placed targets in a controlled shop environment; dynamic calibration is performed on the road.
- Calibration is commonly required after windshield, sensor, bumper, alignment, and collision repairs — confirm in OEM information.
- Correct tires, ride height, alignment, parts, and battery support are prerequisites.
- Document every calibration and verify the feature works afterward.

lessons.title: Post-repair calibration and collision repair
lessons.body:
Collision repairs affect ADAS more than any other type of work. Bumpers, grilles, windshields, mirrors, and suspension parts all carry or influence sensors. A repair that looks perfect can still leave a sensor aimed wrong. This lesson covers planning the repair, following the correct sequence, and proving the systems work before delivery.

## Start with research and a pre-repair scan

1. **Identify the equipped features.** ADAS content varies by trim and option package. Use build data from the VIN where available, a visual check for sensors, and the owner's information.
2. **Pre-repair scan** all modules and save the report. It documents existing faults and reveals hidden damage — for example, a radar reporting misalignment after a minor front impact.
3. **Research OEM repair procedures and position statements.** They define which operations require calibration and which parts must be replaced rather than repaired.

## Repair planning considerations

**Bumper covers and emblems in front of radar**

- The area in front of a radar must remain **radar-transparent**. OEMs may restrict repairs in that zone, limit **paint film thickness** and the number of refinish layers, or prohibit body filler there.
- Metallic paints and aftermarket emblems can affect radar performance. Follow the OEM refinish guidance or replace the part.

**Brackets and mounts**

- A bracket can bend in an impact that barely marks the bumper. Inspect every sensor mount, and replace brackets when the OEM requires it.

**Windshields**

- Use glass that meets the OEM requirements for the camera bracket position and optical quality. Incorrect glass is a common cause of camera calibration failure.

**Wiring**

- Follow OEM wiring repair rules. Some circuits, such as twisted-pair network lines and shielded camera cables, have specific repair methods or must not be spliced.

**Restraint systems**

- Many collisions also affect the **SRS (airbag)** system: impact sensors, seat belt pretensioners, and the restraint module. Follow OEM SRS procedures and replacement requirements separately from ADAS work.

## The correct repair sequence

Calibrations must be performed on a vehicle that is structurally and mechanically correct:

1. Structural and body repairs.
2. Suspension repairs and **wheel alignment** — the thrust line is the reference for most calibrations.
3. **Steering angle sensor calibration**, if required.
4. **ADAS calibrations** — static, dynamic, or both, per OEM procedure.
5. **Post-repair scan** of all modules; clear codes and confirm none return.
6. **Verification road test** to confirm each feature operates as designed.

Calibrating before the alignment is complete means the calibration is referenced to the wrong thrust line and must be repeated.

## Verify function, not just a "calibration complete" message

- Confirm lane markings are recognized and lane keeping responds as designed.
- Confirm adaptive cruise detects vehicles ahead and blind spot monitoring detects vehicles in adjacent lanes.
- Confirm parking sensors and cameras display correctly.
- Never test automatic emergency braking by driving at real obstacles; use OEM verification procedures.

## Documentation and liability

Keep the pre-repair scan, post-repair scan, calibration reports, equipment used, setup measurements, and photos with the repair order. If calibration is sublet to a specialist, the repairing shop is still responsible for verifying that the vehicle leaves with working systems. Give the customer copies and explain any system limitations.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** after a minor rear collision repair, the blind spot warning lamp is on.

- The pre-repair scan showed no blind spot codes. The post-repair scan shows a rear radar misalignment code.
- Inspection finds the left rear radar bracket slightly bent, and the new bumper cover was refinished with more layers over the radar zone than the OEM allows.
- The bracket is replaced, the cover is refinished to the OEM specification, and the rear radar calibration is performed per OEM procedure.
- A road test confirms that vehicles in both adjacent lanes are detected. The codes stay clear.

## Safety

- Verification drives take place in traffic. Use a second person to watch the scan tool and obey all traffic laws.
- An improperly calibrated system can brake or steer unexpectedly; be ready to override it.
- Follow OEM SRS disabling and handling procedures whenever restraint components are serviced during collision repair.

## Key takeaways

- Identify equipped features, scan before repairs, and research OEM procedures and position statements.
- Radar zones on bumper covers have paint and repair restrictions; brackets can bend in minor impacts.
- Follow the sequence: structure, suspension and alignment, steering angle sensor, ADAS calibration, post-scan, road test.
- Verify real-world function and document everything before delivery.

questions.q: Which sensor is most commonly responsible for lane departure warning and lane keeping?
choices: Rear corner radar
The forward-facing camera behind the windshield
Ultrasonic parking sensors
Front long-range radar
questions.explanation: Lane functions need to recognize lane markings, which is a camera task. Lane keeping then acts through the EPS system.

questions.q: A front radar is aimed 1° off. At an object 100 m ahead, roughly how far to the side is it actually looking?
choices: About 0.17 m
About 17 m
About 1.7 m
No measurable difference at that distance
questions.explanation: Lateral error ≈ distance × tan(angle) = 100 × tan(1°) ≈ 1.7 m, about half a lane. Small aim errors become large errors at a distance.

questions.q: Adaptive cruise control is unavailable. The stability control module has an active fault, and the radar has no codes. What is the best first step?
choices: Diagnose the stability control fault first, because ADAS relies on its data
Replace the front radar
Calibrate the front radar
Replace the ADAS module
questions.explanation: ADAS uses wheel speed, yaw rate, and brake control from the ABS/ESC system. A fault there commonly disables ADAS features even when the ADAS sensors are healthy.

questions.q: Which is a requirement for a static forward camera calibration?
choices: Driving on well-marked roads
Heavy traffic for the sensor to learn from
Direct sunlight on the camera
Controlled lighting, a level floor, and targets at specified positions
questions.explanation: Static calibration is done in the shop with targets placed at a specified distance, height, and offset. Uneven floors and poor lighting cause failures or inaccurate results.

questions.q: What distinguishes a dynamic calibration from a static calibration?
choices: It uses printed targets placed in front of the vehicle
It never requires a scan tool
It applies only to ultrasonic sensors
It is performed by driving the vehicle under specified conditions
questions.explanation: Dynamic calibration is started or monitored with a scan tool and completed while driving at specified speeds on roads with clear markings and roadside objects.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence after a collision repair that affected the suspension and the front radar?
choices: ADAS calibration, then alignment, then post-repair scan
Alignment, then steering angle sensor calibration, then ADAS calibration, then post-repair scan and road test
Post-repair scan, then alignment, then ADAS calibration
ADAS calibration, then steering angle sensor calibration, then structural repairs
questions.explanation: Calibrations reference the thrust line and steering center, so the alignment and steering angle sensor must be correct first. The post-scan and road test verify the final result.

questions.q: After a windshield replacement, the forward camera calibration keeps failing even though the target setup is correct. What is a likely cause?
choices: The windshield does not meet the OEM requirements for bracket position or optical quality
The fuel tank is full
The rear radar has not been calibrated
The shop floor has fresh paint markings
questions.explanation: The camera looks through the glass and is mounted to its bracket. Incorrect glass or bracket position is a common cause of calibration failure.

questions.q: Why do OEMs restrict repairs and refinishing on the bumper cover area in front of a radar sensor?
choices: The radar can overheat under extra paint
Radar needs a visible-light view of the road
Paint thickness, extra layers, filler, and some metallic paints can interfere with the radar signal
Bumper covers cannot be refinished at all
questions.explanation: The radar transmits through the cover. Materials and coatings that are too thick or contain metal can weaken or distort the signal.

questions.q: Why must the wheel alignment be completed before most ADAS calibrations?
choices: The alignment clears ADAS codes
Most calibrations reference the thrust line, which an alignment can change
The alignment machine performs the calibration
It is optional if the sensor looks straight
questions.explanation: Sensors must point along the vehicle's actual direction of travel. Changing the thrust angle after calibrating would leave the sensor misaimed.

questions.q: A radar calibration completes successfully. What must still be done before the vehicle is delivered?
choices: Nothing; the scan tool result is sufficient
Disconnect the battery to store the values
A post-repair scan, a verification road test, and documentation
Recalibrate every other sensor as a precaution
questions.explanation: A completed calibration does not prove the feature works. Verify operation, confirm no codes return, and keep reports and setup records with the repair order.

flashcards.back: The system can assist with steering and speed, but the driver must supervise and remain responsible at all times.
Uses camera and/or radar to brake automatically to avoid or reduce a collision.
Behind the windshield near the mirror; it depends on the glass quality and bracket position.
Distance, relative speed, and angle to objects.
76–81 GHz on current systems; some older systems used 24 GHz.

flashcards.front: Effect of a 1° radar aim error at 100 m
flashcards.back: About 1.7 m of lateral error — roughly half a lane width.
Short-range, low-speed sensors in the bumpers used for parking assistance.
Combining data from several sensors, such as camera and radar, for a more reliable view of the road.
In-shop calibration with targets at specified distance, height, and offset, on a level floor with controlled lighting.
Calibration completed by driving at specified speeds on roads with clear lane markings.
The vehicle's actual direction of travel, set by the rear wheels; the reference for most ADAS calibrations.
Windshield replacement, sensor, bracket, or bumper removal, alignment, collision damage, module replacement, and misalignment codes (confirm in OEM information).
The bumper or emblem area in front of a radar, with OEM limits on paint thickness, refinish layers, and filler.
Structure, then suspension and alignment, then steering angle sensor, then ADAS calibration, then post-repair scan and road test.
A manufacturer document stating required scans, calibrations, and part replacement practices for repairs.

courses.title: Hybrid Vehicle Systems
courses.summary: Hybrid architectures and components, high-voltage safety awareness and PPE, the 12 V system and DC-DC converter, and regenerative braking. Hands-on high-voltage work requires certified training, proper PPE, and OEM procedures.

lessons.title: Hybrid architectures and components
lessons.body:
A hybrid vehicle combines an internal combustion engine with one or more electric motor-generators and a high-voltage (HV) battery. Before diagnosing a hybrid, identify its architecture: it determines how the engine starts, how power flows, and which components carry high voltage.

**Important:** this course explains how hybrid systems work so you can diagnose them intelligently. Any hands-on work on high-voltage components requires certified HV training, the correct PPE, and the OEM service procedure for that vehicle.

## Degrees of hybridization

- **Mild hybrid** — a belt-driven or crank-mounted starter-generator, often on a **48 V** system, provides stop-start, light torque assist, and regenerative charging. It generally cannot drive the vehicle on electric power alone. 48 V is below the usual high-voltage threshold but can still deliver very high current, causing arcs and burns.
- **Full (strong) hybrid** — can move the vehicle on electric power alone at lower speeds. The HV battery commonly operates at several hundred volts.
- **Plug-in hybrid (PHEV)** — a larger battery, an on-board charger, and a charge port provide a longer electric-only range.

## Architectures

**Series hybrid**

- The engine drives a generator only; it has no mechanical connection to the wheels.
- A traction motor drives the wheels using battery and generator power.
- Range-extended electric vehicles use this layout.

**Parallel hybrid**

The engine and motor both connect mechanically to the driveline. Motor position is often described with "P" labels:

- **P0** — belt-driven starter-generator on the front of the engine.
- **P1** — motor mounted on the crankshaft.
- **P2** — motor between the engine and transmission, often with a clutch that can disconnect the engine.
- **P3** — motor at the transmission output.
- **P4** — motor driving a separate axle, creating electric all-wheel drive.

**Series-parallel (power-split) hybrid**

- A planetary gearset connects the engine, a generator (often called **MG1**), and the output shaft with the traction motor (**MG2**).
- By controlling MG1 speed, the system varies the ratio continuously — an **electronically controlled CVT (eCVT)**.
- MG1 also starts the engine, so there is no conventional starter.

## Major hybrid components

- **HV battery** (nickel-metal hydride or lithium-ion) with a battery management system, **contactors** (high-voltage relays), and a **service disconnect**.
- **Inverter/converter assembly** — converts battery DC to AC for the motor-generators and back again during regeneration. Some include a **boost converter** that raises voltage for the motors.
- **DC-DC converter** — replaces the alternator and charges the 12 V system.
- **Motor-generators**, **orange HV cables**, and an **electric A/C compressor**.
- Separate **cooling circuits** for the inverter and motors, and air or liquid cooling for the battery.

## Operating behavior every technician must know

- **READY mode:** the vehicle can move silently with the engine off. It is on even if it is quiet.
- **Automatic engine start:** while READY, the engine can start at any moment to charge the battery, heat the cabin, or meet power demand. Never reach into the engine bay while the vehicle is READY.
- **Service or inspection modes:** many hybrids need a scan tool or OEM procedure to keep the engine running for diagnostics or emissions testing.
- **Smart keys:** secure the key away from the vehicle so it cannot be switched on accidentally.

## Worked example: reading power flow

During a gentle stop, a scan tool shows HV battery voltage of **250 V** and current of **40 A flowing into** the battery (the sign convention varies by tool). Using **P = V × I**, the regenerative power is 250 × 40 = **10,000 W (10 kW)**. Watching power flow in data like this helps you confirm whether regeneration, engine charging, and electric drive behave normally (illustrative numbers only).

## Safety

- Treat every orange cable and HV component as energized. Hands-on HV work is for technicians with certified HV training, inspected PPE such as insulated class 0 gloves, and the OEM procedure.
- The engine can start without warning in READY mode; confirm the vehicle is off and the key is secured before working near belts or fans.

## Key takeaways

- Mild hybrids assist; full hybrids can drive electrically; plug-in hybrids add external charging.
- Series hybrids use the engine only as a generator; parallel hybrids connect engine and motor mechanically; power-split hybrids use a planetary eCVT.
- The inverter, DC-DC converter, HV battery, and orange cables are high-voltage components.
- READY means on: the engine can start automatically at any time.

lessons.title: High-voltage safety and PPE
lessons.body:
High-voltage systems in hybrid vehicles can deliver a fatal shock or a severe arc-flash burn. This lesson builds **awareness** of the hazards, protective equipment, and safe work principles. It is **not** a substitute for certified high-voltage training. Only technicians who are trained, qualified, and authorized by their employer may perform high-voltage work, and always with the OEM procedure for that vehicle.

## What counts as high voltage

Vehicle standards such as ISO 6469-3 and UN ECE R100 treat circuits **above 60 V DC or 30 V AC (rms)** as high voltage. Hybrid HV systems commonly operate at several hundred volts DC, and motor circuits carry AC from the inverter.

- HV cables and connectors are identified by **orange** insulation and warning labels.
- The **HV battery is always energized internally**. Opening the contactors or removing a service disconnect isolates the rest of the system, but the cells themselves cannot be switched off.

## The hazards

- **Electric shock** — current flowing through the body, especially hand to hand across the chest, can stop the heart.
- **Arc flash and arc blast** — a short circuit can release intense heat, light, and molten metal, causing burns and eye injuries.
- **Stored energy** — capacitors in the inverter can remain charged for a period after shutdown.
- **Damaged batteries** — electrolyte leaks, toxic gases, and the risk of fire, including delayed thermal events hours or days after damage.

## Training and authorization

- High-voltage qualification is provided through the employer's electrical safety program and manufacturer-specific training.
- A technician who is not HV qualified must not disconnect, open, or probe HV components.
- Routine service on a hybrid — tires, oil, cabin filters — can be performed only while following the OEM precautions for that vehicle, and without touching orange components.

## Personal protective equipment (PPE)

- **Insulated rubber gloves** rated for the system voltage — commonly **class 0** (maximum use voltage 1,000 V AC / 1,500 V DC per ASTM D120) — worn with **leather protectors** over them.
- **Inspect gloves before every use:** check the test date, look for cuts, cracks, and contamination, and perform an air inflation test to find pinholes. Gloves must be electrically retested at the interval the employer's safety program requires.
- **Eye and face protection** suitable for arc flash, and additional arc-rated clothing when the risk assessment requires it.
- Remove rings, watches, and other conductive jewelry.

## Tools and equipment

- A digital multimeter and leads rated **CAT III 1,000 V** (or as the OEM specifies) for measurements.
- **Insulated hand tools** rated for 1,000 V.
- Warning signs, barriers or cones, and a lockbox for the service disconnect and key.
- An **insulated rescue hook** within reach, and a safety observer who knows how to use it and how to call for help.

## Safe work principles (general — the OEM procedure governs)

Only a qualified technician performs these steps, in the order the OEM specifies:

1. Set up the work area with barriers and signs; confirm a trained observer is present when required.
2. Turn the vehicle off (not READY) and secure the key away from the vehicle.
3. Follow the OEM de-energizing sequence, which typically includes disconnecting the 12 V battery and removing the service disconnect, then **locking and tagging** them out.
4. Wait the OEM-specified time for capacitors to discharge.
5. **Verify zero voltage** at the OEM test points using the **live-dead-live** method: prove the meter on a known live source, test the circuit, then prove the meter again.
6. Continue to treat the HV battery as energized throughout the job.

## Damaged vehicles

- After a collision or flood, assume HV components are energized and damaged.
- Follow the manufacturer's emergency response guide and OEM procedures for disabling and handling.
- Watch for smoke, hissing, popping, unusual odors, or heat from the battery area, and store damaged vehicles outdoors, away from buildings and other vehicles, as a general guideline.

## Worked example: recognizing where to stop

An apprentice is replacing a bracket and finds an orange cable connector in the way. The correct action is to **stop** and notify a qualified technician. Removing that connector is HV work: it requires certified training, PPE, a completed OEM de-energizing procedure, and verified zero voltage. Recognizing the boundary is one of the most important skills in hybrid service.

## Safety

- Never touch, cut, or probe orange cables or HV components unless you are qualified and the system has been de-energized and verified per the OEM procedure.
- Never rely on the vehicle being quiet or the dash being dark as proof that it is safe.

## Key takeaways

- Above 60 V DC or 30 V AC is high voltage; hybrid systems operate far above that.
- Hands-on HV work requires certified training, authorization, inspected class 0 (or higher) gloves with leather protectors, and the OEM procedure.
- Verify zero voltage with the live-dead-live method after the OEM wait time.
- The HV battery itself is always live, and damaged batteries can ignite later.

lessons.title: The 12 V system in hybrids
lessons.body:
A hybrid with a fully charged HV battery can still be completely dead if its **12 V auxiliary battery** is weak. The 12 V system powers the control modules, the smart key system, and the circuits that close the HV contactors. This lesson covers how the 12 V system is charged, how to test it, and how to avoid chasing HV faults that are really 12 V problems.

## How the 12 V battery is charged

- Most hybrids have **no alternator**. A **DC-DC converter** — often inside the inverter assembly — steps HV battery voltage down to charge the 12 V battery and run accessories.
- On many hybrids the DC-DC converter operates only when the vehicle is **READY**, not in accessory or ignition-on mode.
- Mild hybrids use a DC-DC converter between the 48 V and 12 V systems.

## Why the 12 V battery matters so much

To go READY, the vehicle must wake its modules, authenticate the key, run self-checks, and close the HV contactors — all powered by 12 V. A weak 12 V battery can cause:

- No READY, or READY that drops out.
- Multiple warning lamps and a list of U-codes and HV system codes.
- Smart key not detected, and erratic gauges or displays.

Those HV-related codes can be **symptoms** of low 12 V voltage, not HV faults. Check the 12 V system first.

## 12 V battery specifics

- Many hybrids use **AGM** batteries, sometimes in the trunk or cabin with a **vent tube** that must be reconnected after replacement.
- Some vehicles have a battery sensor on the negative cable and require **battery registration** with a scan tool after replacement.
- Remote **jump-start terminals** are often provided under the hood. Use only the OEM-designated points.

## Testing the 12 V system

1. **Battery test** with a conductance or load tester set to the correct battery type and rating. Charge the battery first if the tester requires it.
2. **DC-DC converter output:** with the vehicle READY, measure voltage at the battery. It should rise above the resting battery voltage, as a conventional charging system does. Compare with the OEM specification.
3. **Scan tool data:** DC-DC output voltage and current, converter temperature, and related codes.
4. **Voltage drop tests** on the 12 V positive and ground cables under load.
5. **Parasitic draw test:** many modules take a long time to sleep, and telematics units wake periodically. Follow the OEM wait time before measuring.

## Worked example: a no-READY complaint

**Complaint:** the vehicle will not go READY on cold mornings. The scan shows many U-codes and an HV system code.

1. The 12 V battery resting voltage is low, and a conductance test fails. The battery is replaced with the correct type and registered as the OEM requires.
2. With the vehicle READY, voltage at the battery rises above resting voltage and matches the OEM specification — the DC-DC converter is working.
3. A parasitic draw test after the modules sleep shows **0.05 A**. Over three days parked, that draw removes 0.05 A × 72 h = **3.6 Ah** — acceptable compared with the battery's capacity (illustrative numbers; compare actual draw with OEM specification).
4. Codes are cleared and do not return. No HV component was replaced.

Using **P = V × I**, that 0.05 A draw at 12.6 V is only about 0.63 W, but it runs continuously — which is why a small draw can flatten a battery over weeks of parking.

## Jump-starting and charging

- In many hybrids the 12 V battery only **boots** the system; the HV system starts the engine. A jump pack or booster only needs to supply 12 V power long enough to reach READY.
- Many OEMs caution against using a hybrid to jump-start another vehicle. Check the owner's information.
- Use a **battery maintainer** during scan sessions, programming, and extended diagnostics.

## Safety

- Although you are working on the 12 V system, high voltage is present nearby. Do not touch orange cables or HV components; hands-on HV work requires certified training, PPE, and OEM procedures.
- Turn the vehicle off (not READY) and secure the key before disconnecting the 12 V battery. Never disconnect it while READY.
- A 12 V battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a short circuit. Remove jewelry, use eye protection, and protect terminals from tools.
- Batteries can release hydrogen gas; keep sparks away and reconnect vent tubes.

## Key takeaways

- The DC-DC converter replaces the alternator and usually charges the 12 V battery only when READY.
- A weak 12 V battery can prevent READY and set misleading HV and network codes — test it first.
- Verify DC-DC output in READY, check voltage drop, and measure parasitic draw after modules sleep.
- Use OEM jump points, register replacement batteries when required, and keep the vehicle out of READY before disconnecting 12 V.

lessons.title: Regenerative and blended braking
lessons.body:
Regenerative braking turns the motor into a generator that slows the vehicle and recharges the HV battery. It is a major reason hybrids are efficient — and it changes how the brake system is controlled, how it feels, and how it must be serviced.

## The principle

- When the driver lifts off the accelerator or presses the brake, the control system makes the motor-generator act as a **generator**.
- Producing electrical power creates **drag torque** on the driven wheels, which slows the vehicle.
- The inverter converts the generated AC to DC and sends it to the **HV battery**.
- Regeneration happens only on the **axle or axles driven by a motor**.

## Blended braking

Most hybrids use a **brake-by-wire** or electronically controlled brake system to blend regeneration with friction braking:

- A **pedal stroke sensor** and pressure sensors measure how much braking the driver wants.
- The brake control module decides how much of that request comes from **regeneration** and how much from **hydraulic friction brakes**.
- A **pedal simulator** gives the driver a normal pedal feel while the hydraulic unit supplies friction pressure through a pump and accumulator or an electric booster.

## When regeneration is reduced

The system limits or cancels regeneration when:

- The HV battery is at a **high state of charge** and cannot accept more energy.
- The battery is **too cold or too hot**.
- **ABS or stability control** is active — regeneration is reduced so wheel slip can be controlled precisely.
- The vehicle is at **very low speed** — friction brakes complete the stop.
- A fault is detected in the HV or brake systems.

The handoff from regeneration to friction braking can be felt by some drivers. OEMs sometimes release software updates for brake-feel concerns, so check service bulletins.

## Worked example: power during regeneration

During a moderate stop, scan data shows HV battery voltage of **270 V** and **60 A** flowing into the battery. Using **P = V × I**: 270 × 60 = **16,200 W (16.2 kW)** being recovered. If the same stop shows almost no regenerative current, check battery state of charge and temperature data before suspecting a component — a full or cold battery limits regeneration by design (illustrative numbers only).

## Diagnosing brake complaints on hybrids

- **Scan both the brake and hybrid control modules.** Brake codes may originate from HV system limits, and vice versa.
- **Brake feel complaints** such as a grabby pedal at the end of stops: compare with a known-good vehicle, check for software updates, and verify that required sensor initializations were done after previous repairs.
- **Reduced regeneration:** review battery state of charge, temperatures, and HV battery condition data.
- **Friction brake condition:** friction brakes are used less, so rotors rust, pads glaze, and caliper slides and pistons can seize. Inspect them at every service and clean and lubricate hardware per OEM procedure.

## Service precautions

- **Self-pressurizing systems:** many electronically controlled brake systems build high pressure when a door opens, the pedal is pressed, or the vehicle is switched on — even with the vehicle "off." Before opening any brake hydraulic connection or pushing back a piston, disable the system using the OEM procedure (for example, a scan tool service mode or specified fuse removal). High-pressure fluid and moving pistons can cause injury.
- **Bleeding** usually requires a scan tool routine.
- **Pedal stroke sensor and brake system initialization** may be required after pad, sensor, or module replacement.
- **Towing and moving the vehicle:** turning the driven wheels spins the motor, which can generate voltage. Follow the OEM towing instructions, and never rotate the driven wheels with motor HV cables disconnected unless the OEM procedure permits it.

## Worked example: a brake warning after pad service

After front pad replacement, the brake warning lamp is on and the brake module stores a code indicating the system requires initialization. The OEM procedure for this vehicle calls for a scan tool brake system initialization after pad replacement. The technician performs it, the code clears, and the road test confirms normal blended braking and regenerative power in data. No parts were needed.

## Safety

- Disable self-pressurizing brake systems per OEM procedure before brake hydraulic work, and restore them before the road test.
- Brake service on a hybrid does not require HV disconnection, but orange components are nearby. Do not touch them; hands-on HV work requires certified training, PPE, and OEM procedures.
- Confirm a firm pedal and correct warning lamp status before moving the vehicle.

## Key takeaways

- Regeneration uses the motor as a generator, creating drag and recharging the HV battery.
- Blended braking splits the driver's request between regeneration and friction brakes.
- Regeneration is limited by high state of charge, battery temperature, ABS activity, and low speed.
- Disable self-pressurizing brake systems before service, and complete OEM initializations afterward.

questions.q: In which hybrid architecture does the engine drive only a generator, with no mechanical connection to the wheels?
choices: Parallel P2 hybrid
Series hybrid
Mild hybrid
Power-split hybrid
questions.explanation: In a series hybrid the traction motor alone drives the wheels, using power from the battery and the engine-driven generator. Range-extended EVs use this layout.

questions.q: How does a power-split hybrid achieve a continuously variable ratio?
choices: A steel belt running on variable pulleys
A dual-clutch gearbox
A torque converter with a slipping lockup clutch
Controlling generator (MG1) speed through a planetary gearset
questions.explanation: The planetary gearset links the engine, MG1, and the output. Changing MG1 speed changes the relationship between engine speed and vehicle speed — an electronically controlled CVT.

questions.q: A hybrid is in READY mode, silent, with the engine off. Which statement is true?
choices: The engine may start automatically at any moment
The engine cannot start until the key is cycled
The HV system is de-energized
It is safe to reach near the belts and fans
questions.explanation: READY means the vehicle is on. The engine can start without warning to charge the battery, heat the cabin, or meet demand, so keep clear of belts and fans.

questions.q: Vehicle safety standards such as ISO 6469-3 treat circuits above which values as high voltage?
choices: Above 12 V DC
Above 24 V DC or 12 V AC
Above 60 V DC or 30 V AC (rms)
Only above 1,000 V
questions.explanation: Above 60 V DC or 30 V AC rms is high voltage (voltage class B). Hybrid HV systems operate at several hundred volts, far above that threshold.

questions.q: What must a qualified technician do with class 0 insulated gloves before every use?
choices: Nothing, as long as they look clean
Check the test date, inspect for damage, and perform an air inflation test
Clean them with solvent
Stretch them to check elasticity
questions.explanation: Pinholes and cuts may be invisible without an inflation test, and gloves past their retest date are not certified. Solvents and stretching can damage the rubber.

questions.q: After the OEM de-energizing steps and wait time, how does a qualified technician confirm absence of voltage?
choices: Confirm the dash lights are off
Wait an extra hour and assume it is safe
Use the live-dead-live method with a properly rated meter at the OEM test points
Check that the READY light is off
questions.explanation: The meter is proven on a known live source, the circuit is tested, and the meter is proven again. A dark dash or READY light does not prove zero voltage.

questions.q: A hybrid will not go READY on a cold morning and stores many U-codes and an HV system code. What should be tested first?
choices: The HV battery
The inverter assembly
The hybrid control module software
The 12 V auxiliary battery and its connections
questions.explanation: The 12 V system wakes the modules and closes the HV contactors. Low 12 V voltage commonly produces misleading HV and network codes, and it is quick to test.

questions.q: At the bottom of a long mountain descent, a hybrid's regenerative braking feels weaker and the friction brakes do more of the work. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The HV battery is at a high state of charge and cannot accept more energy
The inverter has failed
The 12 V battery is weak
The pedal stroke sensor is out of calibration
questions.explanation: Regeneration is limited when the battery is nearly full or outside its temperature range. The brake module shifts more of the braking request to the friction brakes by design.

questions.q: During a stop, scan data shows 270 V at the HV battery with 60 A flowing into it. What is the regenerative power (illustrative numbers)?
choices: 4.5 kW
33 kW

questions.q: Before replacing brake pads on a hybrid with an electronically controlled brake system, what must be done?
choices: Disable the self-pressurizing brake system using the OEM procedure
Remove the HV service disconnect
Drain all brake fluid from the system
Nothing different from a conventional vehicle
questions.explanation: Many of these systems build high pressure when a door opens or the pedal is pressed. Disabling them per OEM procedure prevents injury and damage; HV disconnection is not normally required for pad service.

flashcards.back: A starter-generator, often on a 48 V system, provides stop-start, light assist, and regeneration; it generally cannot drive on electric power alone.

flashcards.front: Is the HV battery ever fully de-energized?
flashcards.back: No. The cells are always live internally; de-energizing isolates the rest of the system.
The motor acts as a generator, creating drag on the driven wheels and recharging the HV battery.

courses.summary: EV architecture from battery pack to motor, insulation monitoring and the de-energizing process, AC and DC charging diagnostics, and thermal management. Hands-on high-voltage work requires certified training, class 0 gloves and PPE, OEM procedures, and verified zero voltage.

lessons.title: EV architecture: battery, inverter, motor, OBC, and DC-DC
lessons.body:
A battery electric vehicle (EV) replaces the engine, fuel system, and transmission with a high-voltage (HV) battery, power electronics, and one or more electric motors. Understanding what each component does — and where energy is stored — is the foundation for safe, logical EV diagnosis.

**Important:** this lesson explains EV systems for diagnostic understanding. Hands-on work on high-voltage components requires certified HV training, inspected PPE including insulated class 0 (or higher) gloves, and the OEM procedure for that vehicle, including verifying zero voltage before work begins.

## The HV battery pack

- **Cells** (cylindrical, prismatic, or pouch) are grouped into modules, or assembled directly into the pack.
- Packs are commonly in a **400 V class**; some platforms use an **800 V class**.
- The **battery management system (BMS)** monitors cell voltages, temperatures, and current; balances cells; estimates state of charge and state of health; controls the contactors; and reports insulation faults.
- **Contactors** — heavy-duty relays on the positive and negative sides — connect the pack to the vehicle.
- A **pre-charge circuit** (a pre-charge contactor and resistor) charges the inverter's capacitors gradually before the main contactor closes. This prevents a damaging inrush current. A pre-charge fault typically prevents READY.
- **Fuses**, a **current sensor**, and often a **pyrotechnic disconnect** that opens in a crash are built in.
- A **service disconnect** or other OEM-specified isolation point is part of the de-energizing procedure.

## Power distribution and interlocks

- A **power distribution unit** or HV junction box feeds the inverter, on-board charger, DC-DC converter, electric A/C compressor, and HV heaters, each with its own fuse.
- The **high-voltage interlock loop (HVIL)** is a low-voltage circuit that runs through HV connectors and covers. If a connector is unplugged, the loop opens and the system opens the contactors. HVIL codes often mean a connector is not fully seated. **HVIL is not a substitute for the OEM de-energizing procedure.**

## Inverter and traction motor

- The **inverter** converts battery DC into three-phase AC using power semiconductors (IGBTs or silicon carbide MOSFETs). It controls motor **speed** through frequency and **torque** through current, and it converts motor output back to DC during regeneration.
- The inverter's **DC link capacitors** store energy and can remain charged after shutdown until they discharge.
- **Motor types:**
  - **Permanent magnet synchronous motors** — efficient and common; they need an accurate rotor position sensor (often a resolver), which may require an offset learn after replacement per OEM procedure.
  - **Induction motors** — no permanent magnets.
  - **Wound-rotor (electrically excited) synchronous motors** — use a powered rotor winding instead of magnets.
- Most EVs use a **single-speed reduction gear** and differential, often combined with the motor and inverter as an **e-axle**.

## On-board charger and DC-DC converter

- The **on-board charger (OBC)** converts AC from the charging equipment into DC for the battery. Its rating limits AC charging speed.
- The **DC-DC converter** charges the 12 V battery and powers low-voltage loads. The 12 V system still wakes the modules and closes the contactors, so a weak 12 V battery can stop an EV from going READY.

## Worked example: why higher voltage helps

Using **P = V × I** and the power loss in a conductor, **P(loss) = I² × R**:

- Delivering 100 kW at **400 V** requires 100,000 ÷ 400 = **250 A**.
- Delivering 100 kW at **800 V** requires only **125 A**.
- With an illustrative cable resistance of 0.01 Ω, the loss at 250 A is 250² × 0.01 = **625 W**; at 125 A it is 125² × 0.01 ≈ **156 W** — one quarter.

Halving the current allows lighter cables and less heat for the same power, which is one reason some platforms use 800 V (illustrative numbers only).

## Safety

- Treat every orange cable and HV component as energized. Only technicians with certified HV training, inspected class 0 (or higher) gloves with leather protectors, and the OEM procedure may work on them.
- Energy remains in the battery at all times and in capacitors until they discharge. Zero voltage must be verified by a qualified technician before any HV work.

## Key takeaways

- The BMS manages the pack and controls the contactors; the pre-charge circuit protects against inrush current.
- The inverter converts DC to three-phase AC to control motor speed and torque, and back to DC during regeneration.
- The OBC handles AC charging; the DC-DC converter supports the 12 V system that the whole vehicle depends on.
- HVIL opens the contactors when a connector is opened, but it never replaces the OEM de-energizing and zero-voltage verification procedure.

lessons.title: HV safety, insulation monitoring, and de-energizing
lessons.body:
EV high-voltage systems can kill. This lesson explains how the system protects people, how insulation faults are found, and what de-energizing involves. It is an **awareness lesson, not authorization**:

- Hands-on HV work requires **certified high-voltage training** and employer authorization.
- It requires **inspected insulated class 0 (or higher) gloves** with leather protectors, eye and face protection, insulated tools, and a CAT III 1,000 V rated meter.
- It must follow the **OEM procedure** for that exact vehicle.
- **Zero voltage must be verified** before anyone touches an HV conductor.

## An isolated (floating) system

The HV system is **not connected to the vehicle chassis**. HV positive and HV negative are both insulated from the body.

- Because there is no chassis return path, touching one HV conductor and the body does not, by design, complete a circuit.
- If insulation fails on one side (a **first fault**), the system still runs — but a person touching the other side and the body could now complete the circuit. A single fault removes the safety margin.

That is why the insulation must be monitored continuously.

## Insulation monitoring

- The BMS or a dedicated monitoring circuit measures the **insulation (isolation) resistance** between the HV conductors and the chassis.
- If resistance falls below the threshold, the vehicle warns the driver, stores a code, and may prevent READY or charging.
- Regulations such as UN ECE R100 express minimum isolation resistance in **ohms per volt** of working voltage. As illustrative arithmetic only: 500 Ω/V on a 400 V system equals 200,000 Ω (200 kΩ). Use the thresholds in the OEM service information.

## Narrowing down an isolation fault (for qualified technicians)

- **Scan data first.** Note the isolation resistance values and the conditions when the fault appears.
- **Contactors open vs. closed:** a fault present with the contactors open points toward the battery pack side; a fault that appears only with the contactors closed — or only when a load such as the A/C compressor or heater runs — points toward external components.
- **Common causes:** coolant leaks into the pack or power electronics, water in connectors, chafed cable insulation, failed internal insulation in a component, and incorrect oil in an electric A/C compressor.
- **Insulation resistance testing** with a megohmmeter is done only after the system is de-energized and verified, at the OEM-specified points and test voltage.

## The de-energizing process (overview — the OEM procedure governs)

Only a qualified technician performs these steps, in the OEM's order:

1. Set up barriers and signs; inspect PPE, including the glove test date and an air inflation test; have a trained observer and rescue hook available when required.
2. Switch the vehicle off, secure the key away from the vehicle, and disconnect any charging cable.
3. Disconnect the 12 V system as the OEM directs.
4. Open the OEM-specified isolation point (service disconnect or first responder loop) and **lock and tag** it out.
5. **Wait** the OEM-specified time for capacitors to discharge.
6. **Verify zero voltage** at the OEM test points with the **live-dead-live** method: prove the meter on a known source, measure between HV positive and negative and from each to chassis as specified, then prove the meter again.
7. Continue to treat the battery pack as energized; its cells cannot be switched off.

Re-energizing also follows the OEM procedure: covers and connectors installed, HVIL closed, tools removed, and a clean scan afterward.

## Damaged EVs

- After a collision or flood, assume HV components are energized and the pack is damaged.
- Follow the manufacturer's emergency response guide. Signs of **thermal runaway** include smoke, hissing, popping, and heat, and fire can occur hours or days later.
- Store damaged EVs outdoors, away from buildings and other vehicles, as a general guideline, and never attempt to charge a damaged pack.

## Worked example

**Complaint:** an insulation fault warning appears, and the vehicle refuses to DC fast charge.

1. Scan data shows normal isolation resistance with the contactors open, but it drops when the A/C compressor runs.
2. The history shows a recent A/C service at another shop.
3. A qualified technician de-energizes the vehicle per OEM procedure, verifies zero voltage, and tests the electric compressor's insulation resistance at the OEM test voltage — it fails.
4. The oil sample shows the wrong oil type was added. The compressor is replaced and the refrigerant system flushed per OEM procedure. Isolation resistance returns to normal and fast charging works.

## Safety

- If you are not HV qualified, your role is to stop, keep others away, and get a qualified technician.
- Never accept a dark dash, a silent vehicle, or an open HVIL as proof of zero voltage — only a verified measurement is proof.

## Key takeaways

- The HV system is isolated from the chassis; insulation monitoring detects a first fault before it becomes a shock hazard.
- Contactor state and load conditions help locate an isolation fault.
- De-energizing requires certified training, class 0 gloves and PPE, the OEM procedure, lockout, the wait time, and verified zero voltage.
- The pack is always live, and damaged packs can ignite later.

lessons.title: AC and DC charging systems and diagnostics
lessons.body:
Charging complaints are among the most common EV concerns, and many are not vehicle faults at all. A structured approach separates the **supply** (outlet, EVSE, or station), the **connection** (cable, connector, and charge port), and the **vehicle** (on-board charger, battery management, and thermal limits).

## Charging levels and connectors (North America)

- **Level 1 AC** — a 120 V household outlet; slow, useful for overnight top-ups.
- **Level 2 AC** — 208 V (common in commercial buildings) or 240 V (common in homes) through wall-mounted or portable equipment.
- **DC fast charging** — an off-board charger supplies DC directly to the battery through the vehicle's charging contactors, bypassing the on-board charger.
- **Connectors** — SAE J1772 (AC); CCS1, which adds DC pins below the J1772 layout; SAE J3400 (NACS), carrying AC and DC in one connector; and CHAdeMO on some older vehicles. Use only certified adapters.

The wall unit is **electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE)**. For AC charging, it supplies AC power and tells the vehicle how much current it may draw; the actual charger is the vehicle's **on-board charger (OBC)**.

## How AC charging communicates

The SAE J1772 **control pilot** signal coordinates AC charging. Nominal values (general guideline — verify against the standard and OEM information):

- **State A, about +12 V** — no vehicle connected.
- **State B, about +9 V** — vehicle connected, not ready to charge.
- **State C, about +6 V** — vehicle ready; charging permitted.
- **State D, about +3 V** — charging with ventilation required (rare).
- **0 V or −12 V** — no power available or an EVSE fault.

The EVSE advertises the maximum current with the pilot **duty cycle**. Between 10% and 85% duty, available current is approximately **duty cycle × 0.6**; a 50% duty cycle means about 30 A. A **5% duty cycle** signals digital communication, which DC fast charging uses. A separate **proximity** circuit detects the connector and the latch button, stopping charging when the button is pressed.

For DC fast charging, the BMS requests voltage and current digitally, and the station runs an insulation check before energizing the connector.

## Why charging may be slower than expected

- **Battery temperature** — a cold pack accepts much less current, especially for DC fast charging; preconditioning helps.
- **State of charge** — power tapers as the battery fills, often sharply near full.
- **Station limits** — power sharing, derating, or a lower-power station.
- **Supply voltage** — 208 V commercial supply delivers less power than 240 V at the same current.
- **Settings** — charge current limits, schedules, or a reduced EVSE setting.
- **Thermal protection** — charge port temperature sensors reduce power if a connection overheats.

## Diagnosing charging complaints

1. **Define the failure:** Level 1, Level 2, DC fast charging, or all? One station or many? Error messages, time of day, temperature, and state of charge when it happened.
2. **Verify the supply:** try another known-good station or EVSE, or a known-good vehicle on the customer's equipment. Tripped breakers, GFCI trips, and weak outlets are common causes.
3. **Inspect the charge port:** debris, water, bent or discolored pins (a sign of overheating), a damaged latch, and the charge port door and lock actuator.
4. **Scan the vehicle:** OBC, BMS, and charge port codes; pilot duty cycle, proximity status, AC input voltage and current, battery state of charge and temperatures, charge port temperatures, and isolation resistance.
5. **Measure pilot and proximity signals** only with a purpose-built EVSE test adapter or breakout box. **Never probe charge port or connector pins directly** — AC pins can be live and DC pins carry lethal voltage.

## Worked example: slower charging at work

A customer reports charging "much slower" at work than at home on Level 2. Both stations show a pilot duty cycle of about 53%, so 53 × 0.6 ≈ **32 A** is available at each. Using **P = V × I**:

- Home at 240 V: 240 × 32 = **7.68 kW**.
- Work at 208 V: 208 × 32 ≈ **6.66 kW** — about 13% less.

At home, adding 40 kWh takes about 40 ÷ 7.68 ≈ 5.2 hours before losses (illustrative numbers). The vehicle is working normally; the difference is the supply voltage. Explaining this saves an unnecessary OBC replacement.

## Safety

- The charging system is part of the HV system. Hands-on work on the OBC, charge port HV wiring, or DC charging contactors requires certified training, PPE including class 0 gloves, and the OEM procedure with verified zero voltage.
- Always disconnect the charging cable before HV service; a connected cable can energize the system.
- Replace damaged or overheated charge port components per OEM procedure; do not attempt field repairs of HV pins.

## Key takeaways

- The EVSE supplies AC and advertises allowed current; the vehicle's OBC does the AC charging. DC fast charging bypasses the OBC.
- Pilot states and duty cycle reveal what the EVSE is offering and what the vehicle is requesting.
- Many slow-charging complaints are caused by temperature, state of charge, station limits, or supply voltage — verify before replacing parts.
- Use purpose-built adapters for pilot measurements and never probe charge port pins directly.

lessons.title: EV thermal management
lessons.body:
Temperature controls almost everything an EV does: how fast it charges, how much power it delivers, how far it drives, and how long the battery lasts. The thermal management system keeps the battery, motor, and power electronics in their working ranges while also heating and cooling the cabin.

## Why battery temperature matters

- Lithium-ion batteries perform best in a moderate temperature range — roughly 15–35 °C (59–95 °F) as a general guideline; verify the OEM operating range.
- **Cold batteries** accept charge slowly. The BMS limits DC fast charging and regenerative braking to protect the cells.
- **Hot batteries** age faster, so the BMS limits power and charging rate as temperature rises.
- The BMS reports these limits as reduced charging power or reduced performance. Often that is **normal protection**, not a fault.

## System components

- **Coolant loops** — typically a battery loop with cooling plates under or between modules, and a drive unit loop for the motor, inverter, on-board charger, and DC-DC converter.
- **Electric coolant pumps** with variable speed, and **multi-way valves** that connect or separate the loops depending on demand.
- A **radiator** and fans for rejecting heat to the outside air.
- A **chiller** — a heat exchanger that uses the A/C refrigerant to cool battery coolant below ambient temperature.
- **HV heaters** (often PTC heaters) that warm the battery or cabin, and on many vehicles a **heat pump** that moves heat efficiently in either direction. Some systems also use motor waste heat.
- **Temperature sensors** throughout: cell and module sensors, coolant inlet and outlet, inverter, and motor.
- Some older and smaller packs are **air-cooled**, drawing air through ducts and filters that must be kept clear.

## Preconditioning

Many EVs heat or cool the battery on the way to a DC fast charger when the driver selects the charger in the navigation system, or on a schedule. A preconditioned battery charges much faster in cold weather. Customer education about preconditioning resolves many winter charging complaints.

## Diagnosing thermal complaints

- **Typical complaints:** slow DC fast charging, reduced power messages, poor cabin heat, reduced range in cold weather, fans or pumps running after charging (often normal), coolant leaks, and codes for pumps, valves, or sensors.
- **Sensor plausibility:** after a long cold soak, all temperature sensors should read close to ambient and close to each other. A sensor far from the others points to that sensor or its circuit.
- **Coolant level and type:** check level as the OEM specifies and use only the specified coolant; some systems require specific formulations.
- **Air in the system:** trapped air causes hot spots and pump noise. Most EVs need a **scan tool fill-and-bleed routine** that cycles the pumps and valves, often combined with vacuum filling.
- **Active tests:** command pumps and valves with the scan tool and confirm the expected temperature changes in live data.
- **Refrigerant side:** the chiller depends on the A/C system. Low charge or a failed electric compressor can limit battery cooling during fast charging.

## Electric A/C compressor precautions

- The compressor is an **HV component** driven by its own inverter.
- It uses a specific **insulating oil** (commonly a POE type). Contaminating it with the wrong oil, such as conventional PAG, can lower the compressor's insulation resistance and trigger isolation faults.
- Use only the OEM-specified oil and refrigerant, and service equipment designed to prevent oil cross-contamination. In the US, refrigerant handling requires EPA Section 609 certification.

## Worked example

**Summer complaint:** DC fast charging drops to low power a few minutes into every session.

1. Data shows battery temperature rising faster than normal during charging, while the chiller inlet and outlet temperatures barely differ.
2. The coolant reservoir is low, and a small leak is found at a hose connection near the drive unit.
3. After the repair, the OEM fill-and-bleed routine is run with the scan tool. On the next fast-charging session, battery temperature stays within range and charging power follows the normal curve.

**Contrast:** the same "slow charging" complaint in winter, with a cold battery at arrival and no preconditioning used, is normal operation — the fix is customer education.

## Safety

- The electric compressor and HV heaters are high-voltage components. Hands-on work requires certified HV training, PPE including class 0 gloves, and the OEM de-energizing procedure with verified zero voltage.
- Coolant can be hot and the system pressurized; allow it to cool and follow the OEM procedure before opening it.
- Refrigerant handling requires the correct certification, equipment, and eye and hand protection.

## Key takeaways

- Battery temperature limits charging, regeneration, and power; many limits are normal protection.
- EV thermal systems combine coolant loops, pumps, valves, a chiller, heaters, and often a heat pump.
- Check sensor plausibility after a cold soak, use the specified coolant, and bleed air with the OEM scan tool routine.
- Electric A/C compressors are HV components that require the specified insulating oil to prevent isolation faults.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the pre-charge circuit in an EV battery pack?
choices: To balance cell voltages during charging
To charge the inverter capacitors gradually before the main contactor closes, preventing inrush current
To charge the 12 V battery
To heat the battery in cold weather
questions.explanation: Closing the main contactor directly onto discharged capacitors would cause a damaging current surge. The pre-charge contactor and resistor limit that current first; a pre-charge fault typically prevents READY.

questions.q: Which statement about the high-voltage interlock loop (HVIL) is correct?
choices: It is a low-voltage loop through HV connectors that opens the contactors if a connector is opened, but it does not replace de-energizing
It discharges the inverter capacitors
It measures insulation resistance to the chassis
Once it is opened, the HV system is safe to work on
questions.explanation: HVIL is a protective and diagnostic feature. Only the OEM de-energizing procedure with verified zero voltage makes the system safe to work on, and the pack itself always stays live.

questions.q: How much current is needed to deliver 100 kW on an 800 V system?
questions.explanation: I = P ÷ V = 100,000 W ÷ 800 V = 125 A. The same power at 400 V needs 250 A, and because conductor loss equals I² × R, halving the current cuts that loss to one quarter.

questions.q: The HV system is isolated from the chassis. Why is a single insulation fault still treated as serious?
choices: It is not; a single fault is harmless indefinitely
The fault raises the pack voltage
The fault prevents the contactors from opening
The first fault removes the safety margin, so touching the other pole and the chassis could complete a circuit
questions.explanation: With one pole leaking to the chassis, the body becomes part of a possible current path. Insulation monitoring warns of that first fault before a second contact creates a shock hazard.

questions.q: Isolation resistance is normal with the contactors open, but it drops whenever the A/C compressor runs. Where should a qualified technician focus?
choices: The electric A/C compressor and its HV circuit
The battery pack internals
The 12 V battery
The charge port
questions.explanation: A fault that appears only when a specific load operates points to that load. Wrong compressor oil or internal insulation failure in the electric compressor is a known cause.

questions.q: A qualified technician has opened and locked out the OEM isolation point. What must happen before any HV conductor is touched?
choices: Wait the OEM-specified time, then verify zero voltage with the live-dead-live method at the OEM test points
Begin work immediately, since the isolation point is open
Confirm the dash is dark, then begin work
Take one reading with any available meter
questions.explanation: Capacitors need time to discharge, and only a measurement with a properly rated, proven meter at the specified points confirms zero voltage. The pack itself remains energized throughout.

questions.q: An EVSE's control pilot shows a 40% duty cycle. About how much current is the EVSE offering?
questions.explanation: Between 10% and 85% duty cycle, available current ≈ duty cycle × 0.6, so 40 × 0.6 = 24 A (per SAE J1772; general guideline).

questions.q: A customer's EV charges on Level 2 at 32 A both at home (240 V) and at work (208 V), but charging at work is slower. What explains it?
choices: The on-board charger is failing
The pilot signal is faulty
The lower supply voltage delivers less power at the same current: about 6.7 kW versus 7.7 kW
The HV battery is damaged
questions.explanation: P = V × I: 208 × 32 ≈ 6.66 kW and 240 × 32 = 7.68 kW. The vehicle is operating normally; the supply voltage accounts for the difference.

questions.q: In winter, DC fast charging starts slowly and increases as the battery warms. The battery was cold on arrival and preconditioning was not used. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: Replace the BMS
This is normal battery protection; explain preconditioning to the customer
Replace the charge port
The battery chiller has failed
questions.explanation: Cold lithium-ion cells accept charge slowly, so the BMS limits power until the pack warms. Preconditioning on the way to the charger improves charging speed.

questions.q: Which practice helps prevent isolation faults when servicing an EV's A/C system?
choices: Using any PAG oil that matches the viscosity
Adding extra oil to protect the compressor
Using a leak-sealer additive
Using only the OEM-specified insulating oil and equipment that prevents oil cross-contamination
questions.explanation: Electric compressors are HV components whose oil is part of the insulation. The wrong oil can lower insulation resistance and trigger isolation faults.
